So, I am looking for a bit of an intuitive explanation for what is going on here.

The "intuitive" TL;DR is that OLS as a model inherently treats the dependent and the independent variable asymmetrically: only $y$ is assumed to be noisy, while $x$ is assumed to be exact.

I would've expected the fit to go through the center of the data cluster.

I'm not sure where that expectation is violated. The OLS fit does go through the "center", as long as you define the center as the point $(\mu_x, \mu_y)$.

If you want an intuitive understanding of what you observed, you first need to realize, as mentioned already by several contributors, that OLS treats Y and X asymmetrically.

To convince you of this, just plot, on your existing graph, in addition to the OLS line of Y against X, the OLS line of X against Y. You should see a different regression line. The two lines do in fact intersect at the point $(\bar x, \bar y)$ (that is a property of OLS; and that point is the center of gravity of your 2D cloud of points); and you will find that your "intuitive" best fit is somewhere between these 2 lines.

This is because OLS regression of Y against X minimizes the sum of vertical errors, while OLS regression of X against Y minimizes the sum of horizontal errors, but our visual intuition (our pattern matching brain) goes for minimizing the Euclidean (orthogonal) distance: hence the cognitive disconnect.

The plot below illustrates the scenario (it is based on some data I had, looking at the 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) as a function of age), when I was making that very point.

You can clearly see that both OLS regressions are slightly "biased" wrt what one might call the "main axis".

If you want a regression which matches your intuition, then look (as others have mentioned) at total least squares regression, or at Deming regression, or at orthogonal regression.

So the short answer to the question posed in your title is, "because it is supposed to have a bias". But the OLS does go through the center of gravity; just not at the angle our brains would have picked, and that is intentional, given what the OLS does.

As @mkt said this is the difference between OLS and total least squares. The solution to the slope of the line in OLS is $\beta_{ols}= {\sigma_{xy}} / {\sigma_{x}^2}$. What you also did was find the eigenvector with the maximum corresponding eigenvalue (PCA). For TLS we find the line with the smallest eigenvalue, which is the same line as the eigenvectors are orthogonal. The direction line from PCA is $\mathcal{l}(t)=\mu+t v$ ($\mu=(\mu_{x}, \mu_{y})^{T}$, $v$ is the eigenvector $v=(a,b)^{T}$) and the TLS line is $\mathcal{l}(t)=\mu+t (-b,a)^{T}$. These lines differ from OLS as the slope of the PCA line is $\beta_{PCA}=\bigg[\sigma_{y}^{2}-\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sqrt{(\sigma_{y}^{2}-\sigma_{x}^{2})^{2}+4\sigma_{xy}^{2}}\bigg]/{2\sigma_{xy}}$, which is only the same as the OLS slope if $(\sigma_{x}^{2}=\sigma_{y}^{2})$ or $\sigma_{xy}=\pm\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}$ (perfect linear relationship $|\rho|=1$).

From a geometric point of view the linear fit line is the shear/skew angle of an ellipse, while the axis that your brains wants to see is the axis of a rotated ellipse. Although shearing an ellipse creates a rotated ellipse, the angle of the resulting ellipse's axis does not equal the shear angle.

The image below you can see angle difference between the the bounds of the sheared/skewed ellipse (blue parallelogram) and the axes of the rotated ellipse (red dots and lines).

Also, an equivalent transformation (and resulting ellipse) can be achieved by shearing along the x-axis. In this case the shear angle is angle of the regression line where the x-variable contains variation, but the y-variable is fixed.

The answer lies in the data generating process. As other answers have pointed out, the simple OLS model assumes

$$ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon $$

and that $X$ and $\varepsilon$ are independent. It also assumes that we know $X$ with certainty.

Let’s consider the case where we have a perfectly fit regression and all error terms are zero. Because all the data points lie along the regression line, there is no variance in any other direction. So if we were to do PCA on this, the principal component would be in exactly the same direction as our regression line, matching your intuition. Once we start to add noise (i.e. increase the error term), which is strictly in the vertical direction, PCA is going to capture some of that for the first principal component, and leave what’s left over for the second. That is, the direction of maximum variance is going to be more extreme in the $Y$ direction. That’s what you’re observing in your own plots (only talking about the slope discrepancy here, not the centroid, which is covered by other answers).

Now consider the opposite extreme, when error dominates. Here it’s useful to pull apart the variance of $Y$:

$$ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \operatorname{Var}(\beta_1 X + \varepsilon) = \operatorname{Var}(\beta_1 X) + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \beta_1^2 \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) $$

So in the case where

$$ \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) \gg \beta_1^2 \operatorname{Var}(X), $$

nearly all variation is vertical. The principal component direction approaches vertical as error variance increases.

Another source of confusion may be that the covariance ellipse only serves as a meaningful data contour when $(X, Y)$ are jointly normal. Here are examples where $X$ has different distributions:

Again, we see the same pattern: when the $X$ variance dominates, the principal component lines up far more with the regression line. But when the ellipsoid doesn’t coincide with such a tight contour of the data, we can more easily see that we’re dealing with different things in PCA and OLS.

Notice that when

$$ \operatorname{Var}(X) \gg \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon), $$

PCA and OLS align. But the ellipse no longer describes the data's shape. It indicates direction, not density.

Here’s the code used to generate this data. Notice that the make_y_from_x function follows the precise assumptions of OLS. $Y$ is a linear function of $X$ plus i.i.d. Gaussian noise (if you want to have correlated residuals to try to violate the assumption, you can create that in the data generating process). Importantly, $X$ isn’t necessarily a random variable. $X$ could be from an experiment we designed with fixed values, or non-random for any other reason. It can also be random (but still known with certainty), so it’s important to think about this when specifying a model. (See What is a random variable and what isn't in regression models). Notice that the covariance ellipse treats $X$ and $Y$ symmetrically, but the data generating process is quite different.

Quick summary:

  • When $\operatorname{Var}(X) \gg \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)$: PCA aligns with OLS (the textbook case)
  • When $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) \gg \operatorname{Var}(X)$: PCA approaches vertical
  • $X$ is not necessarily random, and definitely doesn’t have to be normally distributed.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse

SLOPE = 1.0
INTERCEPT = -100.0
X_MEAN = 150.0
X_SCALE = 50.0


def make_y_from_x(x, noise_std, slope=SLOPE, intercept=INTERCEPT):
    return intercept + slope * x + np.random.randn(len(x)) * noise_std


def deterministic_binary_x(n):
    x_low = X_MEAN - X_SCALE
    x_high = X_MEAN + X_SCALE
    x = np.repeat([x_low, x_high], n // 2)
    if len(x) < n:
        x = np.append(x, x_high)
    return x


def deterministic_uniform_x(n):
    return np.linspace(X_MEAN - X_SCALE, X_MEAN + X_SCALE, n)


def bimodal_x(n):
    mix = np.random.rand(n) < 0.5
    x = np.empty(n)
    x[mix] = np.random.randn(mix.sum()) * (X_SCALE / 3) + (X_MEAN - X_SCALE)
    x[~mix] = np.random.randn((~mix).sum()) * (X_SCALE / 3) + (X_MEAN + 3 * X_SCALE)
    return x


def triangular_x(n):
    return np.random.triangular(
        X_MEAN - X_SCALE,
        X_MEAN + X_SCALE,
        X_MEAN + X_SCALE,
        size=n
    )


def plot_from_cov(ax, x, y, title):
    x = (x - np.mean(x)) / np.std(x)
    y = (y - np.mean(y)) / np.std(y)

    mu_x, mu_y = np.mean(x), np.mean(y)

    cov = np.cov(x, y)
    eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
    idx = np.argmax(eigvals)

    v = eigvecs[:, idx]
    angle = np.degrees(np.arctan2(v[1], v[0]))

    a = 3 * np.sqrt(eigvals[idx])
    b = 3 * np.sqrt(eigvals[1 - idx])

    ax.plot(x, y, '.', alpha=0.05)

    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    xs = np.array([x.min(), x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, slope * xs + intercept, lw=2)

    ax.quiver(
        mu_x, mu_y,
        a * v[0], a * v[1],
        angles='xy',
        scale_units='xy',
        scale=1,
        width=0.01,
        color='black',
        zorder=20
    )

    ell = Ellipse((mu_x, mu_y), 2 * a, 2 * b,
                  angle=angle, edgecolor='red',
                  facecolor='none', lw=2)
    ax.add_patch(ell)

    xmin = min(x.min(), mu_x - a)
    xmax = max(x.max(), mu_x + a)
    ymin = min(y.min(), mu_y - a)
    ymax = max(y.max(), mu_y + a)

    ax.set_xlim(xmin, xmax)
    ax.set_ylim(ymin, ymax)
    ax.set_aspect('equal', adjustable='box')

    ax.text(0.02, 0.98, title,
            transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha='left', va='top',
            fontsize=11, weight='bold')


# -------- Joint normal: variance domination --------
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
axs = axs.ravel()

n = 20000
beta = 1.0

settings = [
    (0.3, "var(X) >> var(ε)"),
    (5.0, "var(ε) >> var(X)")
]

for ax, (sigma, label) in zip(axs, settings):
    X = np.random.randn(n)
    Y = beta * X + np.random.randn(n) * sigma
    plot_from_cov(ax, X, Y, label)

for ax in axs[len(settings):]:
    ax.axis("off")

plt.tight_layout()


# -------- Different X distributions --------
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
axs = axs.ravel()

make_xs = [
    deterministic_binary_x,
    deterministic_uniform_x,
    bimodal_x,
    triangular_x
]

sigma = 30.0

for ax, make_x in zip(axs, make_xs):
    X = make_x(n)
    Y = beta * X + np.random.randn(n) * sigma
    plot_from_cov(ax, X, Y, make_x.__name__)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

I think the one piece that makes this hard to answer is that these models are trained using whatever state of the art neural model works best, BUT then there is a ton of additional “training” by humans in terms of preferred output. On top of that there are likely additional models for triaging queries so that they go to the correct sub model. All the while, additional tweaking is done in ways that no one might know about apart from the engineers. But let's put that aside.

Things we know:

  1. The training data corpus is so large that there doesn't seem to be any feasible way to ensure that only a single language is represented. Indeed, I think it's reasonable to assume that it would be more efficient to not artificially partition languages and train separate models.

  2. As one of the Redditors mentioned in the link in your question, usually the context surrounding tokens are other tokens in the same language.) So then a logical extension of the examples you give and what was known about word2vec (that it constructs a semantic spatial representation that could operate sensibly with vector arithmetic) is that a conceptual representation could prevail, but I'm not sure how this would be structured geometrically, since, as far as I know, there is no symbolic system on top of any of the commercial LLMs regulating what actual token, and in what language, is outputted.

  3. These models are not static, they are being tweaked all the time. We continue to train them while using them (thanking them for good answers, v. asking for a better answer). In order for them to stay current, they must be fed more training data. In the early days there was some criticism that the training data were skewed heavily toward certain well-represented languages. So there’s that additional variable: these are not static models. They’re always being tweaked. Still the examples do reinforce the idea that they’re attempting to use one giant representation for all language, which would probably need to be the case for translation and transcription services at the very least.

Things we don't really know:

  1. If you subscribe to the connectionist view of cognition, then these models do represent knowledge. I think it's best to view them as vast memory systems rather than knowledge systems, as knowledge tends to include more than linguistic tokens (e.g., schemas, rule-based symbol manipulation, etc.). So if you accept that view, then the vast memory system would show some organization around concepts, and then some mapping to specific tokens. Given the extremely complex deep neural architecture and attention mechanisms, it is very difficult to analyze this formally. The best one can do is to follow other cognitive scientists and empirically test these systems with prompts in a way that would uncover patterns that would suggest a particular representation or organization.

  2. Does training via a transformer-based NN induce quasi rule-based knowledge. This is an extension of the first point, and there is much skepticism about this fact. The skepticism again stems from the classic debate in cognitive science about symbolic cognition v. connectionism.

Personally I would say that this question fits better in the AI or data science StackExchanges. There isn't much statisticy about this question.

The trick is how those algorithms are working and likely they have some sort of filtering process going on – like the variational autoencoders with their latent space.

And to be fair, me as a human in an environment with four languages, I am mixing up words constantly as well. Adding words from different languages is a process that has been happening since ages. It doesn't require computers to do this.

First, linear regression is only linear in its coefficients, not in the variables, so you absolutely can fit a quadratic like so

$$y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1x_{i}+\beta_2x^2_i + e_i$$

That we can approximate anything to a polynomial is a consequence of Taylor's theorem, really, and most often linear or quadratic is good enough for our purposes, they are sufficiently good approximations.

Take the case of economics where linear regression sees ample usage. Here, most often, the question is one of distinguishing correlation from causation (rather than predicting with precision). In this context all we need to know if a change in X entails some significant change in y over some short enough interval that we can easily approximate the (ostensibly) continuous function with a straight line.

@EdM is, of course, correct. And those transformations are very, very flexible.

But let's take a really simple case. One independent variable, one dependent one. And a straight line for the fit (no transformations).

First, it's not a dichotomy between cases where this fits and where it doesn't. Sometimes, this simple straight line is a very good fit to the data; a lot of physics problems are like this. Sometimes this straight line is a terrible fit: Take anything which is sinusoidal, just as one case. If $y = \sin x$ then a straight line will not work at all.

More often, though, it's sort of an OK fit. Remember, as George Box said "all models are wrong, but some are useful." Even in those physics problems the straight line will ignore some issues (e.g. friction, air resistance, whatever). In other cases, there will be a lot of error in the model, and a better fit would be obtained with a more complex model.

A lot of the art and science of data analysis is figuring out how much complexity is "worth". Should we model a transformation? If so, just a quadratic? Or a spline? Perhaps a fractional polynomial. Maybe we need control variables. Moderators. Mediators. Etc.

Or maybe the straight line is enough.

In my view, this isn't a purely statistical question. We have to consider the context. Again, for me, this is what made being a statistical consultant fun.

As for how one tackles such problems, well, what I do is try to figure out what makes sense. Computers make this playing easy. But I try to be careful to not torture the data too much -- and there are ways to avoid that, too.

You’re right: it’s quite an assumption that the world is so simple that it can be modeled with lines, planes, and hyperplanes. But, the…

STONE-WEIERSTRASS THEOREM

…says that, technicalities aside, “decent” functions can be approximated arbitrarily well by polynomials. If you’ve gone far enough in linear algebra, you know that complicated polynomials like $wxz-x^7y^9-wz^2+9w^5x^3yz^8$ can be viewed as linear combinations of basis elements of a vector space. This gives a way to express that polynomial as a dot product of a vector of basis elements and a vector of weights. Across multiple data points, that becomes the familiar $X\beta$ from linear regression.

This is not limited to polynomials. Any linear combination (weighted sum/difference) of functions of the original data can be represented as a dot product. Fourier series can be represented this way to obtain periodicity in the regression fit. Splines can model curvature and can have advantages over polynomials in doing so. You can interact functions of single variables with something like $\sin(x_1)\cos(x_2)$.

Overall, that seemingly simple formulation of linear regression as $X\beta$ can model an enormous amount of complicated behavior.

In the real world, most problems are not linear.

I'm analytical chemist. At least in my field, linear problems are not rare at all. (This answer thus may be seen as illustration to @PeterFlom's and @SextusEmpiricus' answers.)

In the past 100 or 150 years, massive amounts of work went into finding ways of getting measurements/signals that allow linear predictions of the characteristics we actually want to predict (often concentrations or physical values such as viscosity, density, etc.). (With an uncertainty that is sensible for the application at hand.)

(Often even in both meanings of how a model/function can be linear: linear in the parameters ("statistician's linearity") but in addition also linear in the independent variable ("chemist's linearity") - we call these models bilinear in chemometrics.)

The linearity in the independent is often obtained by transformation - e.g. we fit pH = $-\log_{10}$ concentration vs. voltage instead of proton concentration, because there linearity is a sensible approximation for most applications. And if that approximation is not sufficiently good, we move on and use activity instead of concentration (all this is undergrad physical chemistry). Suitable transformations are usually derived by physics and chemistry, but if need be, one can fall back to using generic Taylor expansion as pointed out in some of the other answers. And sometimes, the Taylor expansion comes quite naturally considering the expected function, see below*.

In other words, in analytical chemistry (as well as other similarly "measuring" fields) we actually use hardware and/or software approaches that yield data for the statistical modelling/machine learning that are already cleaned of a lot of the known artefacts that cause deviation from linear behaviour, and that are transformed by external knowledge (physics, chemistry) in ways to yield linear behaviour (again, typically in both meanings - but at least in the stats meaning).

And there are often good reasons to stick to this effort even though it is nowadays computationally feasible to use non-linear models.

  • E.g., in Raman spectroscopy, so-called shot noise following a Poisson distribution means that removing background light optically leads to better sigal to noise ratio compared to measuring Raman signal on top of background light and then subtracting the background light signal later on.

  • In addition, wet-lab science often has small sample sizes, restricting the model complexity we can afford. We just don't have sufficient real data available or they are very expensive to obtain. This is where transformations according to physics/chemistry that lead to data which is known to work with low-complexity linear models really helps a lot.

    (Up to now, pre-trained deep models for "my" types of data are not available)

* Taylor expansion: even there, looking at what kind of function physics (or in other cases, chemistry) suggests can help tremendously. E.g. again Raman spectroscopy: when calibrating the spectrograph's spectral axis i.e., fitting ultimately Raman shift $\Delta\tilde\nu = \tilde\nu_0 - \tilde\nu$ (the difference between excitation and observed wavenumbers) as function of spectrograph pixel number, it turns out to be good to fit first wavelength $\lambda = \frac{1}{\tilde \nu}$. The reason for this is: $\lambda = f(pixel)$ has a sinus expression for grating spectrographs. And the series expansion of $\sin(x)$ is a polynomial with odd power terms only. In spectroscopic reality, we typically allow even terms as well, but check that they get small coefficients in the fit. This can easily be done by a linear model, even with a few reference wavelengths only. In contrast, trying to fit the wavenumber (or Raman shift) directly by a polynomial would be a mess, since polynomials are no good at all for fitting a function that is essentially $\frac{1}{polynomial}$.
(What is sometimes done by a Taylor expansion/polynomial is the correction of an existing spectrograph calibration)

TLDR; There are several reasons that make ordinary least squares (OLS) popular, and that's why many problems are approached with that technique (it doesn't necessarily make the problems inheritly linear).

Why can many problems be looked at as linear and "just about trying to find a solution for the Equation Ax = b"?

A lot of these problems are not 'linear' (depending on how you consider linear).

  • OLS regression, the equation $y = X \beta$, is only linear in the parameters $\beta$.

    It can capture non-linear relationships between $y$ and some variable $x$ by having non-linear functions of $x$ in the columns of the matrix $X$.

    See also:

    • How to tell the difference between linear and non-linear regression models?
    • Why does ordinary least squares have to be linear in the parameters?
    • When will point ($\bar{x}$, $\bar{y}$) not go through the regression line?

  • Non-linear relationships can appear approximately as linear or polynomial functions. A polynomial OLS regression might be applied to it, but that may not be the true underlying relationship. See Interpreting logistic modelling and linear modelling results for the same formula

  • Relationships can be linearized by transforming the variables such that the transformed problem is linear in the parameters.

    This linearisation is often performed to make computations easier. For example:

    • excel uses a linearisation to compute exponential relationships
    • Before people had a lot of computation power people used graphical methods to fit equations and straight lines are easy to estimate. Fitting the Michaelis Menten equation is an example.

With more computation power and a lot of data linear methods become less necessary (that's what this question ponders about: Why do we use Linear Models when tree based models often work better than linear models?). But simple linear or quadratic relationships still provide easy interpretable relationships.

Despite what they might tell you, it's not that "so many problems are linear", it's that we settle for linear approximations when the nonlinear versions are too difficult. They don't necessarily answer the exact question we want to ask, but we settle for them because the exact questions we want to ask are too difficult to answer.

For example, with your own example of linear regression, often the quantity you're actually interested in minimizing is absolute deviation (L1 norm) rather than squared deviations (L2 norm). But whereas squared deviations are trivial to minimize (just set the derivative equal to zero and you get a linear equation with a unique solution), absolute deviations don't give you an easy-to-solve equation when you differentiate them. So, traditionally, people have given up and settled for squared deviations.

Of course, nowadays, with computers and better algorithms, minimizing absolute deviations is easier than it used to be, but it's still hard to do, and depending on your particular problem you are still likely to settle for squared deviations.

Having excess precision gives the illusion that it is real. This is more a point for communication than anything else though.

For example, let's say you did need age to the hour. And when the data was recorded it was recorded in years to 5 decimal places. So someone looks at that and assumes that it is actually accurate and then goes and uses it. But in fact it was just recorded to the day, and then silently converted to 5 decimal place fractions of a year. Now they have incorrect data. Of course this is a silly example as basically nothing needs age to the hour except astrology.

A more realistic example (I think that I saw in a book on communications). If a recipe says "1 cup of flour" then the user knows it is pretty rough and isn't going to stress too much. If the recipe says 116 grams of flour, the user assumes that every gram counts; otherwise why would it be given. Even though 116 grams is actually 1 cup*. These quantities expressed differently can result in different actions. In the former case if the cup isn't perfectly level the baker isn't going to put too much effort in; in the latter they might.

In scientific fields data often does come with measurement errors listed, so it is precise about the precision. Not so much for data we use day to day.

*: normal approximation is 120 grams, but i have heard specific numbed given from 116 to 135 grams for a particular brand of flour at a particular climate.

Does this matter for statistical purposes?

That depends massively on the kinds of statistics and modelling and the use case.

For many usecases not explictly accounting for precision is entirely in-appropriate. But that is not a problem with the precision of the data you input but with not taking it into account at all.

If the data is entered with mixed precision where some entries are rounded to the day and some accurate to the minute, then that could cause problems for some ML methods. Consider in for example if the precision was linked to a particular client (e.g. different say hospitals using different software) uploading the data, then a ML method could learn to distinguish which client was used based on the precision. There is a great story about a researcher who trained a image recognition model to predict chance of death based on scans of MRIs got good results. Someone ran a feature importance algorithm on the data and it came back that the most important part was the top corner, where the time was printed into the image. Turns out if you are getting an MRI at 2am, something is very wrong and your survival chances go way down. We can imaging similar things being detected if there is a pattern in the mixed precision.

For lots of things though it just won't matter, because the summary statistics like means and std-dev will be rounded themselves and its all just too far beyond the decimal place.

In general, communication is part of doing statistics well. So I think my first point about giving illusion of real precision is most important.

Realistic example: Oil drop experiment.

Millikan measured the charge on an electron by an experiment with oil drops... He got an answer which we know now was off: he gave a very, very precise value with small error bars. Problem? He got the viscosity of air wrong.

If you look at measurements of the charge of the electron over time, the value slowly but steadily reaches the correct value, one error bar at a time.

This is not because scientists didn't discover right away that Millikan got the wrong value, as they did. But they questioned their results instead of his, and would redo the experiment until they got numbers that fit inside of his error bar, so with the same level of precision.

So what problem does too much precision cause? It makes readers incorrectly assume that your data is more accurate then it actually is. That can make it harder for future information preformed with a greater accuracy/precision to correct your values, as science tends to assume that the published result is right, and the unpublished result wrong. Because of scientific process, peer review etc...

1. You're wasting computer memory and computational power. But that is extremely cheap.
  2. People summarize the data with an excess of precision, which takes up more space, uses more ink and paper, but most importantly increases the cognitive load on the reader. But that's really the problem of the person summarizing it.

I can't think of a real problem. In my (real) work we store dates as the number of milliseconds or microseconds since the Unix epoch began (1st January, 1970). A problem we often come across is that you're not sure if someone stored in milliseconds or microseconds - but it's relatively obvious if your database query says that someone has been employed for thousands of years, you got it wrong.

Occasionally it feels like dramatic overkill, for example, we see that someone started a task at 1743524254154 and ended it at 1743524256154 then it took 2.5 seconds. But anything else would be less consistent and more prone to error, and errors are expensive (especially compared to memory and computation).

I think it could cause issues, at least in limited situations.

Let's say you are doing a study involving newborns at the hospital. For your purposes, you collect their age in days, but for whatever reason, you decide to convert the value to years.

Let's say you collect the data for two infants born yesterday. For your purposes, they are both one day old, but were actually born several hours apart. In your database, this would be 1 day / 365.2425 ≈ 0.002737907 years.

There are a few potential issues that I can think of to be aware of:

  1. The first is unrelated to your question, but I'll point it out here anyway: what conversion factor are people using to convert to years? Is it consistent within/across datasets? I used 365.2425, but someone else could easily have used just 365
  2. If you decide to round aggressively (e.g., to 0.0027, or four decimal places), this could cause regression issues, depending on what the rest of your data looks like. The error introduced by rounding is pretty high for a one-day-old infant, especially compared to, say, a 100-day-old infant. If the error introduced by rounding is more or less consistent across samples, then it should be less of an issue. If you're dealing with adults instead of infants, then the error of going to four decimal places is probably a non-issue.
  3. This is where we get to your main question. For the original purposes I outlined above (a study of infants in the hospital with ages measured in days), having more precision shouldn't hurt something like a basic regression. However, because of the conversion, retaining more digits of precision implies your initial measurement has a higher precision than it actually did (i.e., hours, minutes, or seconds, instead of days). This might cause issues with something like clustering algorithms; I'm not sure but wouldn't be surprised. More importantly, if the initial level of precision (days) is not adequately communicated, someone else might take the data and use it under the assumption that it is more precise than it really is. So let's return to the two infants born several hours apart. Someone else might be studying infant outcomes in the hours after birth. They might see your data and assume it has the hourly precision they need, and, without direct access to the original birth records, just assume they were twins. That could cause regression issues, despite having more digits recorded in the database. Now, depending on what the whole dataset looks like, there could be patterns in the values to indicate what's going on, but I wouldn't assume everyone would catch that.

So the biggest issue with more digits recorded in the data is the risk that it implies more precision than the original measurement had. Whether or not that causes issues is situational.

As the discussion indicates, there is more about false precision that doesn’t matter than that does matter. In data analysis I can think of only two real ramifications of false precision. First, it may lead the analyst to report statistical estimates with false precision. For example an analyst may report a mean age in years to 5 digits if the data were reported in years and fractions of a year to 4 digits. Second, when using a semiparametric model, model intercepts are created to coincide with observed values of the dependent variable. Semiparametric models span the spectrum of discrete measurements all the way to truly continuous measurements. Software such as the R rms package orm function completely removes the computational problem, e.g., one can get virtually instant analyses with an unlimited number of distinct levels of Y, but the false precision will create actual parameters in the model, one per distinct observed level of Y. Again, there are no downstream bad consequences of this, just more parameters in the model that don’t affect power or precision of statistical estimates (standard errors of $\hat{\beta}$. Rounding Y to its real precision will speed up computations by a fraction of a second if desired.

Regarding having too much precision in X rather than Y, there are no consequences I can think of other than making it easier to choose knot locations in spline fitting due to fewer tied X values.

There’s a general principle that you should only round once, at the end.

During the steps of your calculation you should retain all possible accuracy (working with the maximum number of decimal points or significant figures possible). But ideally you should then perform a rigorous error analysis, to calculate how precise each result is. Then when you report a numerical quantity, you will also report on the precision (the ± uncertainty or error bars) and hence will present it with appropriate rounding.

This will also be covered in most introductory undergraduate physics lab manuals (like here or there). At a higher level you might use Bayes to produce confidence contours for nonlinear multidimensional results.

If you round multiple times (i.e., at multiple intermediate stages of the analysis) you will accumulate more error in your final result.

In short

  1. The relationship (where we wouldn't refer to $x/y^2$ as an interaction term)

    $$z \sim ax+by+cx/y^2$$

    can be approximated by

    $$z \sim a'x+b'cy+c'xy$$

    and in practice, when people are doing ordinary regression, they just stick with a regular linear expression plus potential secondary polynomial terms.

  2. If you have an idea – based on theory – about some more precise equation, then sure, use that instead.

You should consider the collinearity between predictors

Broadly speaking, when we have predictor variables that are strongly collinear (i.e., strongly correlated) they will tend to give a lot of overlapping information that leads to additional variance in the relevant model coefficients for those predictors in the regression model. Consequently, when designing experiments and models, ceteris paribus, we generally prefer to use predictor variables that have less collinearity. In some cases we use principal components of sets of predictors to achieve this, but this is something that is usually weighed off against ease of interpretation.

In the case of height and weight, there is a substantial amount of collinearity from the fact that increases in height generally add to all dimensions of the body, and thus lead to higher weight. Measures like BMI, CI, etc., seek to decompose these two things by measuring "mass relative to height" in some reasonable sense. Because there is an attempt to account for the direct impact of height on weight, and then judge mass relative to height, these measures are much less strongly correlated with height than is weight.

For this reason, one reasonable approach in regression analysis of this kind is to incorporate height as one predictor and some measure of "relative weight" (e.g., BMI, CI, etc.) as the other predictor. In your case you would want to add these for both parents, with height acting as the moderator variable and the remaining "relative weight" being the predictor of interest.

Some final advice in a study of this kind: (1) just as it is possible to decompose parental size into "height" and "relative weight", it is likewise possible to do this for the baby, so you could consider building a bivariate regression that decomposes "birth size" into height/length and relative weight of the baby and treats both as response variables in the regression; (2) it will be important to obtain data on key confounding factors that will have a strong causal impact on the birth size (especially gestation time).

Does the interaction term necessarily need to be exposure × moderator?

If you want an interaction terms in your model, then it makes sense that it would be the interaction of the exposure and moderator. There is a complication in the present case because BMI, CI, etc., are not perfect representatives of "relative weight" and are already somewhat correlated with height (BMI more than CI). The interaction term is likely to capture some of the imperfection in the measurement of "relative weight", but you should be able to get reasonable results with a reasonably simple interpretation.

If an interaction term coincides with an existing formulae (i.e., BMI), is it necessary to add its components as main effects in statistical models, given that the "interaction term" is often used as a standalone variable in statistical models?

Not only is it not necessary to add its components, but adding both components (as in your Option 5) will create significant problems with collinearity and interpretation. If both weight and BMI are added as exposure variables in addition to the moderator height then you are effectively adding both absolute and relative weight, and you will get a complex output that is decomposing the linear effects of both absolute and relative weight as joint predictors. This is likely to make interpretation of your results significantly more difficult.

I want to add, in conjunction to the other answers, that BMI is just a quadratic model for the mass of a human body,

$$m(L) = \alpha L^2.$$

The BMI of a person, usually measured in kg/m², is the constant $\alpha$.

Although mass truly scales with the cube of a linear dimension ($m \propto L$) for solids (volumes), human bodies do not. When Adolphe Quetelet first studied height and mass in the 19th century, he observed that body mass grew more slowly than $\propto L^3$. Statistically fitting

$$\text{mass} \propto \text{height}^k $$

in adult populations yields exponents $k$ typically between about 1.1 and 2.5. Often we find $k$ near 2, rather than 3.

If every part of a human body "grew" proportionally with height, they would have constant shape and density, and indeed $m \propto L^3$. But human proportions change with stature. Taller people tend to be relatively more slender (less "chunky") than shorter people, so volume grows more slowly than $L^3$. An index based on mass∕height² correlates more directly with heat loss, basal metabolic rate and, crucially, body‑fat percentage.

BMI is a phenomenological model. There are other multiparameter models that are not pure black‑box polynomials, and that rest on first principles (geometry of cylinders, cones, ellipsoids; mixture densities; electrical conduction laws). The only phenomenological step in these models is fitting the remaining constants to real‐world data.

Some models from first principles yield the quadratic BMI model: if we assume that the legs must support the torso under compressive stress without exceeding bone strength, and that

$$\sigma =\frac{mg}{A} \approx \text{constant},$$

where $A$ is the cross‐sectional area of the femur (or combined support area), then $A \propto m$. But then $A \propto L^2$, so

$$m \propto L^2.$$

If one instead assumes that bones behave like elastic columns that must resist buckling under body weight, we can derive a quartic model. Using Eulers buckling criterion

$$F_\text{crit} \propto \frac{EI}{L^2}, \quad I\propto d^4,$$

and fixing material properties (Young's modulus $E$ and density), one finds

$$m \propto L^4,$$

at least this applies to the mass of an individual limb. This is the approach of McMahon 1.

Imposing a maximum physiologically acceptable tendency to sag (N.J. MacKay's version of McMahon's approach 2) shifts the exponent into

$$\frac{7}{3} < k < \frac{8}{3}.$$

His then argues, based on minimization of the mass moment of inertia about an axis through the hip joints and and heat loss considerations, that $k \approx \frac{8}3$ for growing children.

Real bodies are not homogeneous, though. Partitioning mass into compartments can make more sense. In the classic 2‑compartment model you measure total body density (e.g. underwater weighing or air‐displacement plethysmography) and solve for

$$\text{fat mass} + \text{fat‑free mass} = \text{body mass},\quad \frac{\text{body mass}}{\text{body volume}} = \frac{\text{FM}}{\rho_{\text{fat}}} + \frac{\text{FFM}}{\rho_{\text{FFM}}}.$$

One can extend the model to 3 or 4 compartments by measuring total body water (via isotope dilution) and bone mineral (via DXA), each with its own density or hydration constant.

You could also move beyond "mass vs. height" models, as there are whole families of multivariable anthropometric and body composition models that combine circumferences, lengths, skinfolds, bioimpedance, etc.

Unfortunately, BMI is as easy to calculate as it is a poor measure of adiposity. Not only that, but the denominator ($m^2$) may benefit more by being a cube ($m^3$). Moreover, anecdotally, in all the studies I've worked on in cancer epidemiology, BMI was a poorer predictor compared to other measures of adiposity such as waist or hip circumference or waist-to-hip-ratio (and just as easily measured as BMI).

From a purely information power, any of the models with the interaction and the main effects is going to be more powerful than having BMI. I very much agree with other's suggestions of using a quantile regression for this problem, provided you have a healthy sample size.

Measure theory relates to probability theory because "probability" is defined as a normed measure (i.e., a probability measure). In practical statistical work, we don't usually work directly with these measures and the sigma-fields for their domain. Instead we work with density functions that relate to these probability measures. We use the probability measure whenever we go back and compute probabilities for events of interest in the model.

In regression analysis the model form defines a conditional density for the response variable conditional on the explanatory variables, so a typically Gaussian regression model uses the conditional density function:

$$p_{\mathbf{Y}|\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{y}| \mathbf{x}) = \text{N}(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{x} \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma \mathbf{I}).$$

The resulting probability measure is related to this conditional density by:

$$\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{Y} \in \mathscr{Y} | \mathbf{x}) = \int \limits_\mathscr{Y} p_{\mathbf{Y}|\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{y}| \mathbf{x}) \ d \mathbf{y} = \int \limits_\mathscr{Y} \text{N}(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{x} \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma \mathbf{I}) \ d \mathbf{y}.$$

Whereas the density function has a single real input argument $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the probability measure has an input argument $\mathscr{Y} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ which is a set of values that is an element of a corresponding sigma-algebra. Typically we are working with real numbers so the sample space is the set $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the sigma-algebra is the corresponding class of Borel sets on $\mathbb{R}^n$. When we are doing statistical analysis we usually don't mention measure theory or the sigma-algebra that the probability measure is defined on, but it is there in the background.

So in a mathematical sense, is the sigma algebra from measure theory related to the variables in $\bf{X}$, or is that just related to the error term $\bf{\epsilon}$?

It may become easier to see if you write the regression as a multivariate normal distributed variable

$$\mathbf{Y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}, \mathbf{\Sigma})$$

which maybe you can see better now, that this is a definition for a probability measure.

A sigma algebra is a set with all intervals/regions $$\prod_{i=1}^n (a_i \leq y_i \leq b_i)$$ and all their their unions. Such intervals describe the events to which we can assign probabilities.

A general, rigorous framework for regression problems can indeed be constructed.

Consider a family of stochastic kernels $\{P_\eta\}_{\eta~\in(a,b)}$ on $(\mathscr Y, \boldsymbol{\mathfrak B}) ,$ that is, for a fixed $B\in\boldsymbol{\mathfrak B}, ~\eta \mapsto P_\eta(B)$ is a measurable map. Let $Y$ be a random variable with values in $\mathscr Y$ and is influenced by regressor $X$ taking values in in $\mathscr X$ with $(\mathscr X, \boldsymbol{\mathfrak A}) .$

Denote by $\mathsf C(\Delta,\mathscr X) $ the class of functions that are continuous in $\theta$ and measurable in $x$ (it is assumed that $\Delta$ is a separable metric space). The regression function $g: \Delta\times \mathscr X\to (a, b), ~g\in \mathsf C(\Delta,\mathscr X)$ determines the distribution of the observation $Y$ given the value of the regressor, that is, if $X=x, $ the distribution of the observation $Y$ is $P_{g_\theta(x) }.$

Regression models involve both cases of regressors: one where $X$ is random and one it being non-random.

When $X$ is random, the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X=x,$ as discussed above, is given by $\mathsf K_\theta(~\cdot\mid x) =P_{g_\theta(x) }.$ If the marginal distribution of $X$ on $(\mathscr X, \boldsymbol{\mathfrak A}) $ is denoted by $\mu, $ then each independent pair $(Y_i, X_i), ~i\in\overline{1, 2,\ldots, n}, $ has the common joint distribution is $$\mathcal L(Y_i, X_i) =\mathsf K_\theta\otimes \mu.$$

In case of non-random regressors, an experimental design fixes the values $x_i\in\mathscr X;$ the observations $Y_i$s are independent with corresponding distributions being $P_{g_\theta(x_i) }.$

When $\theta, x\in\mathrm{l\! R}^d$ and $g_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x, $ the regression problem obtained is linear. When $g_\theta(x) =\varphi(\theta^\top x), $ where $\varphi$ is continuous, then the regression problem obtained is generalized linear.

The updates do not happen layer by layer. We first compute the gradient, which is the partial derivative of the loss function with respect to all of its parameters, i.e. with respect to all its weights and biases. Then the gradient is used to update the weights. A very simple method would be to just subtract the gradient from the weights, scaled by the learning rate, in order to minimize the loss function.

Ok so why is backpropagation done layer by layer? In neural networks the output depends in a layered way on the inputs. So if you calculate the partial derivatives, you have to use the chain rule each time you reach a new layer. Here I will show an explicit example. I will use a dumb activation function $\sigma(x)=\tfrac 1 2x^2+1$ of which it is easy to calculate the derivative: $\sigma'(x)=x$. In the following the input is $x$ and the output is $z_2$. I give every intermediate step a name to make the chain rule clearer.

\begin{align} y_1&=w_1x+b_1\\ z_1&=\sigma(y_1)\\ y_2&=w_2z_1+b_2\\ z_2&=\sigma(y_2) \end{align}

I now want to calculate the partial derivative of the output, $z_2$, with respect to $w_2$. How much does the output change if I wiggle $w_2$ and keep the rest constant? \begin{align} \frac{\partial z_2}{\partial w_2}&=\color{red}{\frac{\partial z_2}{\partial y_2}} \color{orange}{\frac{\partial y_2}{\partial w_2}}\\ &=\color{red}{\sigma'(y_2)} \cdot \color{orange}{z_1}\\ &=\color{red}{y_2} \cdot \color{orange}{z_1} \end{align} If you're familiar with the chain rule this step should have been easy to follow. Let's now calculate the partial derivative of $z_2$ with respect to $w_1$, which is one layer deeper. \begin{align} \frac{\partial z_2}{\partial w_1}&=\color{red}{\frac{\partial z_2}{\partial y_2}} \color{green}{\frac{\partial y_2}{\partial z_1}} \color{blue}{\frac{\partial z_1}{\partial y_1}} \frac{\partial y_1}{\partial w_1}\\ &=\color{red}{\sigma'(y_2)} \cdot \color{green}{w_1} \cdot \color{blue} {\sigma'(y_1)} \cdot x\\ &=\color{red}{y_2} \cdot \color{green}{w_1} \cdot \color{blue}{y_1}\cdot x \end{align}

What do we notice? The factor $\color{red}{\sigma'(y_2)}$ appears in both expressions. This is nice because when calculating the gradient for $w_1$ we can store this value so we can reuse it when calculating the gradient for $w_2$. This sounds like a small efficiency gain, but for the structure that neural networks use this is huge. Each value is reused multiple times because each node is the input to every other node in the next layer. At least in dense neural networks. But for other architectures the speedup is still large.

Backpropagation is nothing more and nothing less then efficiently reusing values when calculating partial derivatives. The whole layer-dependency thing is taken care of by the nature of partial derivatives. To summarize, when performing an update step you first calculate the gradient, which is just a vector containing all partial derivates of the parameters you want to update, and after that you use the gradient to update the weights in a smart way.

in backprop you compute gradients based on current forward pass then update all weights together so when you are computing ∂z/∂w for each layer you use the values before any updates happen so the chain rule still holds you only update after calculating all the gradients

I agree with Sextus Empiricus' explanation (+1 to their answer), though my conclusion is a little different. Much confusion on this topic arises from a mishmash of different frameworks of frequentist inference: Fisher's and Neyman-Pearson's. Null Hypothesis Significance Testing can be thought of as an inconsistent mix of the two or a third alternative, depending on your perspective.

The Fisher and Neyman-Pearson views are individually coherent but mixing them together leads to confusion and illogical practice. The Neyman-Pearson framework is focussed on making decisions, and in this case the alpha level (whether 0.05, 0.01, or anything else) needs to be specified in advance, and the decision followed accordingly. This guarantees long-run error rates in the decisions taken are 'controlled' at a defined level. In the Fisher framework, the p-value is just a continuous measure of evidence and so specific thresholds like 0.05 don't matter.

Because such thresholds have no consequence in the Fisherian view, there are no important consequences to choosing an arbitrary one after doing the analysis. Doing so can help with concise communication; saying $p$ < 0.01 is simpler than $p$ = 0.0036. Otherwise, it doesn't really help or hinder because the threshold does not alter interpretation and this is not a formal decision-making framework. But in a Neyman-Pearson decision framework, making an alpha threshold choice after analysis does cause a major problem: you no longer control your long-run error rates with the specified alpha level, because you have modified your alpha after seeing the result of your analysis.

In your case, the multiple-choice question is poorly worded, which is why some of the answers here disagree. What we need to know to provide a definite answer is what the pre-defined alpha level is. But this is not stated in the question and instead we're left to guess, with two leading possibilities:

  1. If we assume that you have a Neyman-Pearson pre-commitment to an alpha threshold of 0.05, adding a new alpha threshold of 0.01 post-analysis is not legitimate and so option E is invalid. Option B is then the best answer. Note that whether the p-values are called 'small' or 'large' in options A-D is irrelevant, since the question specifies 0.01 < $p$ < 0.05.
  2. If instead we assume that alpha is undefined in the question, then options A-D are automatically invalid because we do not have an alpha with which to take a binary decision. That leaves us only with option E. This is a defensible answer. But I'm uncomfortable with it because option E loosely implies that the alpha was defined after doing after the analysis, which, as we've established, is wrong.

So I vote for option 1 and B as the best answer. But this is a poorly-written multiple-choice question and it demands editing for clarity.

In null hypothesis testing where a choice needs to be forced*, we have a predetermined boundary/threshold, the significance level $\alpha$, that is used to determine whether a p-value is considered small or large.

One issue with the option E is that it sounds a bit as if the $\alpha$ level has been decided afterwards. But in practice, these levels should be decided beforehand.

Compare the following two

  • Do not reject the null hypothesis for α = 0.01.

  • If we had chosen α = 0.01, then do not reject the null hypothesis.

The first sentence leaves it a bit open that α is a predetermined level. (and it happens! that people decide on α after they computed p-values)

Another issue is that sometimes there is not really a rejection or non-rejection of a null hypothesis, and instead just an update of our beliefs about the null hypothesis. In scientific journals you see this often where results are marked with star symbols *, ** or *** depending on whether the p-value is below a certain boundary. It is more an indicator for strength of evidence, than a measure to decide about reject versus non-reject.

An important note is that these $\alpha$ levels can be arbitrary but in certain practical contexts they make sense. E.g. some company that tests a batch by sampling a few cases and only needs an accept/reject answer.

A problem with $\alpha$ levels is that not everything is in this dichotomous situation with 'one test' and 'one non-reject/reject decision'. Testing procedures and gathering data can be iterative. If a scientific journal only accepts certain results with $p<\alpha$, then what's going to happen is that multiple scientists are going to try, or one is going to try several times, until they hit $p<\alpha$ (which due to the implicit multiple testing, and publication bias, does not create the strength of evidence that we think it did).

The description is arguably correct, but potentially somewhat misleading.

While it's not the arithmetic mean of the absolute differences from the mean, there's more than one kind of average. The standard deviation is a root mean square distance from the mean*, one of the family of power means (inverse power of averages of powers). There are more general classes of 'average' still (e.g. replace power with some other function, typically monotonic). The power means include harmonic means as a special case and geometric means as limiting case.

To be less misleading without adding much detail (hopefully additional detail is to be added later when such an explanation is offered), you could say it's a kind of average, one that puts more emphasis on larger deviations. As a result, it is always at least as large as mean deviation.

In terms of variance, that is an ordinary average of squared distances, the ordinary second moment about the mean.

Why describe it as any kind of average? It provides a relatively intuitive sense of what its trying to measure and conveys at least something of how. A more complete sense comes from examining its relationship to a variance and understanding that as an average.

The natural student question is why use this slightly complicated kind of average rather than the ordinary mean deviation? There are some good answers to that question on site already, of course; I think the most compelling reason is because of some special properties of variances, in large part due to the very simple way that variances of sums of values can be written in terms of the individual variances and covariances, the latter of which disappear when you have independence.

* in terms of samples, more strictly this would be the version without Bessel correction. For population quantities it's correct. I'll stick to population (and uncorrected sample-) quantities here.

When attempting a brief explanation of the SD I use a similar phrase but I replace "average" by "typical." Given a chance to follow up with a second sentence I will qualify that by stating "as an approximate rule of thumb, 'typical' means about two-thirds of the data (or distribution) will lie within 1 SD of the mean and very little will lie beyond 2 SDs of the mean."

(For those who believe this characterization applies only to Normal distributions, you are correct insofar as it is derived from Normal distributions, but it is far more general than you might think, applying even to rather skewed distributions. You might find the analysis and commentary at https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/116913/919 to be illuminating.)

This phrasing is imprecise but it's nevertheless accurate insofar as it goes. Experts here know that "very little" is often around 5% for distributions with tails shaped like a Normal distribution, that in extreme cases (which I invite you to characterize ;)) can be 0%, but it is never greater than 25% (by Chebyshev's Inequality).

Experts will also know to be careful not to bait and switch: it's invalid to use an estimate of the SD to make such a statement about the underlying distribution. If that's the intended application, then we need a further qualification: "... assuming the estimated SD is close to the true SD."

As one of the comments said, this is a "hand wavy" first order approximation of what a standard deviation more or less represents. It is not perfectly accurate and I've never seen standard deviation defined this way in a textbook (if a textbook did use this definition without qualification I agree that would be bad). However, there are lots of times where rigorously insisting on only giving technically precise definitions of statistical concepts can be a huge barrier to statistical communication and pedagogy, and where the use of informal (but technically imprecise) definitions can be enormously useful. And this is one of those cases.

A truly accurate definition of standard deviation would just be a translation of the mathematical formula for computing a standard deviation into "normal" English. Something like this: "Take the first observation in the data and subtract the mean from it, and then you take that value and square it. Repeat this for every observation in the data, and then add all of those values together. Then divide that result by the number of observations (or that number minus 1 if you are talking about a sample as opposed to a full population), and then you take the square root of that whole thing."

This not only involves some more complicated mathematical concepts like square roots, and the idea that squaring a negative number makes a positive numbers, but it also just takes a lot of words. For lots of statistical concepts this isn't a problem, because the only people who are going to be using them are going to just be looking at the equation anyways, and they know what a "big sigma" means and how to read the equation.

But standard deviations are such a basic concept in statistics that they are going to crop up in a lot of important contexts (political polls, drug trials, program evaluation) that people who don't know any statistical concept more complicated than an average might come across. If the word "standard deviation" means literally nothing to you, then you are going to have a tough time understanding even basic statistical results. If I found two results with the same mean but vastly different standard deviations, then it is important to convey that those are really different things!

If you are trying to get a reporter to understand what a polling result means, or a policymaker to understand the results of an evaluation study or epidemiological survey or drug trial, then taking five seconds to say something like "it's the average distance of each observation from the average" could be the key to generating real understanding. In contrast, insisting on giving the full definition might prevent them from actually understanding the underlying results. Realistically, their eyes will probably just glaze over and they will ignore you until you start speaking English again. And then (in some cases) they will go make a decision which could impact millions of lives without fully understanding your result.

I've also used this "imprecise" definition when presenting standard deviations to students in intro stats classes. I first provide the full formula and run through the calculations, but I then encourage them to see that what this formula is doing is "kind of showing you how far, on average, each point is from the mean." For many students this technically wrong definition helps them to intuitively grasp the equation that I just showed. Some people, even really smart people, have a tough time with even simple equations - they can understand them with effort, but they often need a bit of help to wrap their head around what is going on. Instead of just writing those people off I've found that using a bit of "inaccuracy" in my initial presentation can help figure out the basic concept, and once they have that it's easy to then say "now here's why what I said doesn't quite work..."

As others have said in the comments, it's tricky to give a definition to someone with little knowledge of statistics without sacrificing accuracy, precision, or comprehensibility. Moreover, a mathematically precise description of the procedure for calculating standard deviation does little to convey the intuitive sense of why we calculated it: in other words, what does it tell us about our data is more important than "what would you need to type into your calculator". Especially when these days most people are just going to look at output from their statistical software anyway!

For example, your explanation to a layperson certainly shouldn't venture into the thickets of whether to apply Bessel's correction or not: while using an $n$ or $n-1$ in the formula can give two slightly different numerical answers, that does little to alter the practical interpretation of the result. And if the answer to your research question did change substantially depending on which of the two you use, then something has probably gone wrong!

So there's no point trying to explain the precise "recipe" you need to follow — realistically we should limit ourselves to trying to describe what the result "tastes like". In other words we are bound to accept some imprecision: a certain quantum of handwaving is necessary and even desirable for our audience to grasp something of how statisticians conceptualise and interpret the SD in daily usage, even if that leaves them unable to calculate it for themselves.

The problem comes if this imprecision also induces inaccuracy, or a tendency to mislead. For example I would strongly avoid saying:

(BAD) The SD measures how far, on average, each data point is from the mean value.

This sounds too much like you are specifying the recipe, and that the SD is calculated in the same way as the mean absolute deviation.

One way to maintain the accuracy of the definition is to "lean in" to the imprecision and just be upfront about it. Fortunately, if you give people a prod to the memory banks, many will recall from high school that there are different "averages" you can calculate. Syllabuses often cover at least "mean, median, mode" but depending on background some may also have seen root mean square, mid-range or trimmed mean. So avoid talking about "the average" and try to talk about "one way of averaging" instead. (Unfortunately, when it comes to which way, the people who already know about RMS, e.g. people whose education specialised in electrical engineering, will likely already understand SD! But if they hadn't seen the link before, then you have a cheap way of giving them extra precision in the definition without sacrificing its comprehensibility.)

Alternatively, avoid the potential confusion between "average" and "mean" by substituting another word entirely, something like:

(BETTER) The SD is one way of measuring how far a typical data point is from the mean value.

This kind of formulation is suitably handwavy about the technical details you don't want to get bogged down in, while acknowledging (at least strongly suggested by "one way of...") that other ways of measuring average distance from the mean exist too. But you could even hint at other measurements of spread that don't use the concept of distance from the mean at all!

(MY PREFERRED FORMULATION) The SD is one way to measure how spread out your data is — it works by finding how far each data point is from the mean value, then averaging these distances out in a particular way to find the 'typical' distance a point is from the mean.

I'd avoid mention of "averaging" if I was not confident my audience had come across the concept of different types of average. But in that case some other tweaks are needed, e.g. "mean value" likely has to become "average value" too. Fortunately I live in a country where, by age 16, students are supposed to have seen mean, median and mode at school. But this does not always apply e.g. to international clients, or people old enough to have gone through an earlier school syllabus which had less emphasis on stats, or who have simply forgotten what they did get taught!

I might also try to strengthen the intuition by suggesting that usually "most" data should lie within one SD of the mean value, that the "vast majority" should lie within two SDs, and "almost all" should lie within three or four SDs. But since I don't want to suggest that the normal quantiles always apply, while the bounds from Chebyshev's inequality could be misleadingly conservative compared to practical data, I tend not to get too bogged down with suggestive percentages.

Things like this always depend on how one defines it formally. This description is accurate under a certain interpretation of "average" and "how far". The standard deviation is the square root of the expectation of the random variable, $(\mathbb X - \mathbb E[\mathbb X])^2$:

$$\sigma := \sqrt{\displaystyle\int_\Omega (\mathbb X(\omega) - \mathbb E[\mathbb X])^2 \; \mathrm d \mathbb P(\omega)}.$$

If $\mathbb E[\mathbb X]$ if not defined, then $\sigma$ is left undefined.

It is rightly called "an average" because we integrate over all $\omega \in \Omega$; in this case we "weigh" quadratically how much $\mathbb X$ differs from $\mathbb E[\mathbb X]$, and then we "sum" all those contributions up.

In general mean absolute deviation is bounded by the standard deviation, as evidenced by Jensen's inequality:

$$\left(\mathbb E \left[ |\mathbb X -\mu| \right]\right)^2 \leq \mathbb E \left[|\mathbb X - \mu|^2\right] = \operatorname{Var}(\mathbb X),$$

where $\mu = \mathbb E[\mathbb X]$.

There is an interesting special case when $\mathbb E \left[ |\mathbb X -\mu| \right]$ and $\sigma$ are essentially the same. If $\mathbb X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu = 0$, then

$$\mathbb E \left[ |\mathbb X -\mu| \right] = [ \mu = 0 ] = \mathbb E \left[ |\mathbb X| \right] = \sqrt{\frac{2}\pi} \sigma.$$

In this case they only differ by a factor.

Dividing by $n-1$ is designed to give an unbiased estimator of the population variance because you do not know the population mean $\mu$ and using $\bar x$ instead might otherwise give a estimate which is on average too low.

The following are correct, though you rarely see the second: $$\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{n} = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{n} - \bar x^2 = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{n} - \left(\frac{\sum x_i}{n} \right)^2$$ $$\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{n-1} = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{n-1} - \frac{n}{n-1}\bar x^2 = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{n-1} - \frac{\left(\sum x_i\right)^2}{n(n-1)} $$

Dividing by $n-1$ rather than by $n$ is done ONLY when $s^2$ is used as an estimate, based on a random sample, of the variance of a population from which one has only a small random sample of size $n.$ If one knew the value of $\mu,$ the population mean, rather than only of $\overline x,$ the sample mean, then one would use $\mu$ rather than $\overline x$ and one would divide by $n$ rather than by $n-1.$

When you use the first you are computing an unbiased estimator for a data sample (estimator). Although you can compute the second, it will be biased.

When using the second you are are computing the variance of a population (descriptive statistic), for which the first is not a good expression.

No. A phrase like "mean of squares minus the square of means" is a description of a formula for the population variance — not the sample variance. (E.g., you can see it suggested here, with a recommended acronym of "MOSSOM"). We see:

$$\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n} = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{n} - \bar{x}^2$$

The mnemonic known to the OP describes the rightmost expression here. This is called the "calculating formula" because it takes fewer operations to produce, and it was an important technique when all such calculations were done by hand (not so now with available technology). To be clear, both of the expressions above produce the exact same number — if you were to double-check with both, and get different results, then that indicates an error in some hand calculation.

However, this reflects the definition for population variance (it has $n$ in the denominator), so it will of course produce a different value than the formula for sample variance noted by the OP (which has $n - 1$ in the denominator, that is, Bessel's correction).

Note that sample variance also has an analogous calculating formula, but it cannot be described by the same MOSSUM mnemonic:

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1} = \frac{\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2/n}{n - 1}$$

By a bit of algebra one can show that $$ \frac 1 {n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline x)^2 = \frac1{n-1} \left( \left( \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 \right) - n \overline x^2 \right). \tag 1 $$ If you evaluated these two expressions and got different values, possibly the problem is that $ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 $ and $ n \overline x^2$ are so close to each other by comparision to their sizes that information was lost by rounding when you subtracted. For example, $1\,000\,000.0317$ and $1\,000\,000.0321$ may both be rounded to $1\,000\,000.32,$ so when you subtract, you get $0.$ But the difference that got rounded to $0$ is the information that you need. One divides by $n-1$ ONLY when using the sample variance as an estimate of the population variance.

The mean of the squares minus the square of the mean is what line $(1)$ above would give you if you had $n$ rather than $n-1$ in the denominator. That is the variance of a distribution that is equal to each $x_i$ with probability $n.$

This is a great question because it is such a confusing topic!

The word "variance" has several slightly different meanings. It is important to understand what these meanings are and to distinguish between them.

  • Meaning 1. Variance is the second central moment of a distribution. This moment may or may not exist, depending on the distribution. $Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$, where $E[X]$ is the expected value of $X$.

  • Meaning 2. Variance of the normal distribution is the second parameter of the distribution. In the normal distribution, it so happens that the second parameter of the distribution (typically denoted by $\sigma^2$) is equal to the variance of Meaning 1. Because of this coincidence, the second parameter of the normal distribution is called "variance".

Note that variance, in both Meaning 1 and 2, is a distribution quantity. This means that it is generally not known, unless you are dealing with a textbook problem, which states its value. Although the variance is typically not known, it could be estimated from the data. Thus, we have Meanings 3 and 4:

  • Meaning 3. Variance is an estimator of the variance from Meaning 1 or 2. Please recall that there are many estimators of variance. These estimators are not equal to each other. Because each estimator has its own advantages and disadvantages, some statisticians might prefer one over another. Or, there might be situations in which a particular estimator is called for. The point is that there is no single estimator -- there is more than one.

  • Meaning 4. Variance is an estimate of the variance from Meaning 1 or 2 that uses one of the estimators from Meaning 3. (An estimator is a formula. An estimate is a numeric result of applying the formula to the data.)

Let's get back to the first part of your question.

The formula $s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$ is one particular estimator of variance (Meaning 3).

The phrase that you give is "Mean of the squares minus the mean squared". For clarity, in my opinion, it is better stated as "Average of the squares minus the average squared", because the word "mean" also has multiple meanings. This phrase gives a different estimator of variance (also Meaning 3).

The first estimator is often called the "unbiased estimator of variance" -- you should be aware that the word "unbiased" here does not mean what it means in regular non-statistical speech. In statistics, "unbiased" is not necessarily a desirable quality. This variance is also called the "sample variance", although I think this term is confusing.

The second estimator is the "method of moments estimator of variance" or, if we are dealing with the normal distribution, the "maximum likelihood estimator of variance". It is also called the "population variance", although I, again, think that this term is confusing.

These are just two common estimators and there are others. Each estimator leads to a different estimate (Meaning 4). Each estimator (Meaning 3) leads to a different estimate (Meaning 4) of the same unknown quantity (Meaning 1). The actual variance (Meaning 1) is never known, it can only be estimated. Different approaches to estimation lead to different estimates (usually they are only slightly different).

Now, to answer your question.

  • In introductory classes, they tell you to use the "unbiased" estimator -- that's the formula that you give. A lot of statistical software and spreadsheets also use this estimator by default.

  • A lot of statisticians prefer the maximum likelihood estimator. For the normal distribution, that's the phrase that you give. The phrase is also the method of moments estimator regardless of the distribution. Method of moments is fine if you don't have a better estimator. But if you do know what the maximum likelihood estimator is, many statisticians would prefer that. (To be clear, the maximum likelihood estimator and the method of moments estimator are the same for the normal distribution. But for other distributions, the maximum likelihood estimator could be very different.)

PS. For some distributions, such as the Cauchy distribution, variance (Meaning 1) is undefined. Thus, the only valid estimator of variance (Meaning 3) is that it is undefined. You can plug data into formulas and get estimates (Meaning 4). But these estimates will not be estimating anything valid or useful, since the actual variance (Meaning 1) does not exist. You can get a number, but the number does not mean anything.

A big point of multiple linear regression is that, while each individual feature may be a weak predictor of an outcome of interest, but several of those can make for quite strong predictions. In that regard, screening out a variable, even in a linear model, due to low correlation with the outcome is problematic. It could wind up ruling out all of the candidate features or at least many that would help you make better predictions.

Once you start modeling nonlinear relationships, either through transformations (e.g., polynomials, splines) or through nonlinear models like random forests, then a model using just one feature might be a perfect predictor of the outcome despite zero correlation between the feature and that outcome, such as $y=x^2$ when $x$ is symmetric about zero. Thus, screening out features due to low correlation with the outcome is a really problematic approach for techniques that consider these nonlinear relationships.

Therefore, I generally find it problematic to rule out candidate feature due to low correlation between them and the outcome of interest.

In addition to the points made, another is that x1 could be involved in an interaction that is strongly predictive, and it's nearly always a mistake to include an interaction without both main effects.

This applies to linear as well as nonlinear models, and is often a big point in trees (and related0 where x1 might be important only for a subset of the data.

I don't know where you learned that using correlation this way is sensible, but I would discount anything else you learned from that source.

A better question would be "is it ever valid to use correlation for feature selection". One case I can think of is where you use correlations among your predictors as a way of cutting down on the number of variables; I don't know if this is the best method, but it's at least reasonable.

As is pointed out in other answers, correlation between a single variable and the response variable does not take into account that the dependence can become greater depending on the values of other variables.

Measures of conditional dependence try to measure this effect, and it is thus a better idea to base feature selection on such measures, rather than on correlation. For regression problems and only metric (or binary, but not multilevel categorial) features, one particular approach is FOCI. It has the nice property that it is model-free and takes care of arbitrary functional dependencies, not just linear relationships like correlation or partial $R^2$.
