A few points:

  1. p values can be calculated for lots of different models. These make different assumptions.

  2. Multiple linear regression does assume normal errors, but, as Glen points out in a comment, the validity of p values depends on several conditions - how extreme is the violation? How big is the sample? etc.

  3. Errors are never perfectly normally distributed. The p values of various tests for normality will give significant results (i.e. say that normality is violated) for very slight violations of normality when N is large. These slight violations will have very little effect on the validity of p values. A quantile plot can be more useful.

  4. If you are really worried, there are regression models that do not assume normality, e.g. quantile regression, robust regression.

  5. There are quite a few people, including me, who think significance is over-emphasized in looking at results of tests.

  6. Despite all the above, many people will report p values even when the assumptions of the model (whether multiple regression or something else) are grossly violated. At one extreme, I had a professor in grad school (my degree is in psychometrics) who said 'If you don't understand the statistics, just report the p value. That's what matters.' (NOTE: This is a description of how badly some people mess up. It is NOT a recommendation, to say the least.)

As others have said, p-values can be calculated for many types of models (or tests that don't directly tie to regression models like, say, some permutation or rank tests).

However, when the assumptions of some model or test are badly violated, the model or test might not answer the question you are interested in or have an inflated type I error rate etc. The assumption of normality of the residuals of a linear regression is one of the assumptions that can to some degree be violated without it mattering too much for modest sample sizes, as long as the deviation isn't too much. E.g. I would not worry all that much about using linear regression for the change from baseline in HbA1c, even though we know that theoretically the residuals cannot possibly be normally distributed (because it is a number $\geq 0$). On the other hand there's situations where a linear model just doesn't make any sense (e.g. time-to-event with right-censoring, unordered categorical outcomes), is very debatable (e.g. binary outcome), or only works well after transformations (e.g. something like the urine albumin-creatinine ratio or viral load really wants to be log-transformed).

There's some experience involved in knowing what situation you're in, so it's hard to give general advice. If you are lucky people have already looked into your particular setting and clearly articulated why it should be analyzed in a particular way (and hopefully they are right about it...).

Especially in cases where the sample size is small (in hundreds instead of in millions), p values of coefficients in linear regression should be doubted when the distribution assumptions of errors are not met or examined. In fact, any asymptotic inferential statistic (e.g., standard error, t statistic, confidence interval) is questionable if the error distribution deviates too much from a normal distribution.

The best practice under nonnormal error term in linear regression includes

  • Use robust standard errors and associated significance test. In R, this is typically done by the sandwich and lmtest packages.
  • Use weighted least squares if the error variance is related to one or more predictors, or generalized least squares if the error terms is correlated, so that the normalized error is normally and independently distributed. In R, this can be examined in nlme::gls()
  • Use bootstrap confidence intervals. For mean statistics like the expectation of a coefficient, the student bootstrap confidence interval performs the best. It collects the sample distribution of the t statistic and finds the threshold from the observed distribution instead of a theoretical t distribution.
  • Use permutation p value. To simulate the results under $H_0: \beta = 0$, permutate a predictor randomly (sample the row number without replacement) many times, estimate the model with each permutated sample $j$, record each point estimate $\hat{\beta}_j$ of that predictor. Estimate the model again with the regular sample to get $\hat{\beta}$. Calculate p value as $p = \sum{I(|{\hat{\beta}_j}| \geq |\hat{\beta}|)} / (1 + \sum_{j=1}^J{1})$. That $1 + $ in the denominator is necessary because $\hat{\beta}$ is considered as one observation in the permutated samples. It also prevents $p = 0\text{ or } 1$ in practice.

More important than using the above methods is to figure out why the error distribution is not independently identically normal.

  • Is linear regression a proper choice? There are generalized linear regression and additive models specifically designed for binary, nominal, ordinal, integer, limited, and censored responses.
  • Is the linearity assumption appropriate? We should test functions of the predictors (e.g. square, cube, logarithm, smooth curve, interactions) to ensure that the model specification (the model formula) is sufficient.
  • Are observations independent? Correlated errors often occur in time series (serial correlation) and stratified sampling (clustered errors).

If yes to all above three questions, we may attempt the four remedy methods.

I think you are conflating multiple things here.

  1. P-values are not specific to the normal distribution. A P-value is just the probability of a random variable being more extreme than a specific value; it can be applied to all distributions. You don't need a T or Z statistic to compute a P-value.

    It's often convenient to be able to assume a specific distribution in order to quickly compute a P-value from the statistic in a single step, but it is by no means required. If you are not feeling confident that your regression coefficients are in fact normally distributed, you can always just perform some sort of simulation or re-sampling/cross-validation to get a non-parametric P-value. See eg. this article on the subject.

  2. You keep referring to the errors being normal, but the P-value of the coefficients isn't concerned with the distribution of the errors! It's about the distribution of the coefficient itself. I'm pretty sure you can have a scenario where the errors are not normally distributed, but the coefficients are.

    For example, consider the popular $L_2$ or Ridge regularization approach with the objective function to minimize being the $L_1$ (ie., mean or total absolute) error. This framework, as-is, assumes a Gaussian prior on the coefficients themselves, and a Laplace distribution for the residuals. It's entirely conceivable to me that with the appropriate underlying generative process (specifically Laplace-distributed residuals and many random factors influencing whether each predictor influences the target), you would get just this picture. This would legitimagely allow you to compute P-values from the T-statistic of the coefficients, although the errors wouldn't be normally distributed.

    E.g., here's a piece of code demonstrating normally-distributed coefficients and non-normal errors, which is achieved by directly defining the underlying generating distributions of both variables:

X = np.random.normal(size=(1000, 100))
error = np.random.laplace(scale=0.1, size=1000)
y = X @ beta + error

beta_hat = minimize(
    lambda betahat: np.abs(X @ betahat - y).mean(),
    np.zeros(100)
)

I'm writing specifically about the p-values regarding coefficients in a linear regression model under normality assumption for the error term; other answers are correct stating that p-values can be computed under all kinds of other model assumptions including nonparametric ones.

To be precise, the p-value is computed under the null hypothesis. It measures the compatibility of the observed data with the null hypothesis, or more precisely of the specific aspect of the data that is measured by the test, which here is a regression coefficient.

Note that the normal and other assumptions refer to the null hypothesis, but the test does not assume that the null hypothesis is true (otherwise it wouldn't be necessary to run a test in the first place). Therefore, technically, p-values are valid (as long as they are computed correctly) regardless of whether model assumptions hold for the observed data or rather the real process that has generated these data.

Even if model assumptions don't hold in reality, the p-value regards a comparison of the data with the null model (in which assumptions hold), and technically there is nothing wrong with that.

The problem is rather the interpretation of the p-values. A very low p-value indicates an incompatibility of the data with the null model. It does not indicate that a specific alternative model is true (like a normal linear regression model with the tested coefficient nonzero). The standard interpretation of a significant test result is that "there is evidence that the true regression coefficient is nonzero", implicitly assuming that the normal linear regression model in fact holds and there is a true coefficient. This interpretation requires the model to hold in the real situation in which the test is applied (but see below), not the computation of the p-value!

One may think that the data can also be incompatible with the null model by violating the normal or some other assumption, and of course, if this were the explanation for the low p-value, the low p-value couldn't be interpreted as evidence that the regression coefficient (defined within the normal model) is nonzero. This is a problem, because we run the test in order to make statements about the regression coefficient, rather than other issues. S. Greenland et al. argue here that significance tests based on p-values in fact test all model assumptions together, not just the (regression coefficient) hypothesis of practical interest.

This may make the test seem useless, but in fact it isn't. The thing is that the test statistic is defined in such a way that it investigates incompatibility with the null model regarding the regression coefficient, and it will reject specifically if the estimated regression coefficient looks to large in absolute value compared to what is expected under the normal null model.

This means that significant rejection can in fact be interpreted, without assuming anything, as saying that "the estimated regression coefficient looks too large (in absolute value) compared to what is expected in the standard normal regression model".

The subtle and difficult question is then, are there models (like for example a regression model with non-normal errors) in which you have in fact a zero regression coefficient of interest (or basically any distributional pattern that you'd describe as "the corresponding x-variable has zero impact on the response"), and where the p-value based on the normal linear regression null model can easily be significant? In this case it would be a misinterpretation of the p-value to say there is significant evidence that the regression coefficient is nonzero. In other cases, even if model assumptions are violated, it would not be a misinterpretation in the above sense - there would indeed be evidence that the x-variable has impact that can be approximated by a nonzero coefficient in a linear model (even though this approximation may not be very good, for example in case of a true positive but nonlinear relationship).

In fact, regarding the specific regression problem, it is rather hard to set up true models that fulfill the above condition, i.e., there is a true zero relationship, but the probability that the normal regression p-value is significant is substantially larger than the significance level, say 0.05. It is possible though. I think it will require a leverage point, i.e., an observation that is far away from the others in x-space. Leverage points have a big impact on regression (including p-values), and if you have a heavy tailed error distribution and a leverage point, I suspect that the probability that the leverage observation will make the p-value significant is larger than 0.05. I also suspect that without leverage point(s), it will be very hard to construct a model with non-normal errors and zero regression coefficient that does this. Such things can be found out experimentally simulating observations from such models (I don't have the time to do this for this answer).

Note also, however, that heavy tailed error distributions, outliers and the like, can much more easily affect the test power, i.e., you may get insignificant p-values in a situation in which you'd say, knowing the true model, that the x-variable actually has an impact, i.e., the test should reject. This may be a problem in practice, although it doesn't make the p-value technically invalid, because it just then says that the size of the estimated regression coefficient alone doesn't constitute evidence against the null model - it doesn't mean there is evidence that the null model is true (insignificant p-values never mean that).

I think that the standard regression p-values are in principle OK even if model assumptions are not fulfilled. They do correctly what they do, and we just need to understand what they can do and what they can't do (and in some situations, obviously, other techniques such as robust regression are better at what we want to do). Key is to interpret them carefully having in mind the potential impact of violations of model assumptions. Given a p-value, visual model diagnostics (like looking for leverage points and their influence, e.g. using Cook's distance) can tell you much about whether significance may have been caused by other reasons than a meaningful impact of the x on the response (I should say, though, that robust regression estimation such as the MM-estimator will give you better diagnostics, particularly making it possible to see that observations at certain leverage points are really not in line with the general trend).

I'm generally comfortable with interpreting a significant p-value that requires some model assumptions if the "message" of the p-value is in line with what clearly can be seen in visual analysis of the data, even if model assumptions look violated (in ways that don't mislead the test).

Actually I think (and know from some experiments) that violations of the independence assumption between errors can much more easily push the p-values into significance without true impact of the x-variable under consideration. And such violations may be hard to detect. At least as much care should be into thinking about and diagnosing potential dependences as into investigating the error distribution.

It is also important to acknowledge that statistical models are idealisations and will never be true. It is therefore not the correct question to ask whether "model assumptions hold" (we know without testing that they don't; therefore formal assumption misspecification tests like normality tests are of very limited informative value); rather we need to investigate whether what goes on in the specific situation has the potential to lead to a misleading interpretation of a test result. Unfortunately this is harder than just running a model assumption test and stating that "we're fine" if the assumption isn't rejected (also there is the misspecification paradox that states that testing a model assumption by some misspecification test and only running a test requiring the model assumption if the misspecification test doesn't reject the assumption will violate the assumption automatically).

Your friends may disagree to the point of name-calling, but the probability is $1/3$ and not $1/2$. Here's a picture to demonstrate:

This probability tree shows the entire setup, and allows you to determine the probability of any outcome -- there are only six possible draws after all (arranged as "columns" in the image above). For example, you can see that indeed exactly half of the possible outcomes have at least one gold ball, and half of them have at least one silver ball. Once you've drawn the first ball there isn't any probability associated anymore to the second draw: there's only one option left within any given box.

However, the "paradox" is that you are being asked about a conditional probability: the first ball in this case was gold. This restricts the outcome space to the ones highlighted in green. It's as if the others don't exist anymore: their paths could not possibly have brought you here. You could not have picked the box with two silver balls, nor could you have picked the silver ball from the box containing both colors first. In the given scenario there's a probability of $2/3$ that the next ball will be gold (Bertrand's original framing of the puzzle), and $1/3$ that it is silver.

The only difference between Bertrand's original description and your problem is that in the former the probability for the second "ball" (actually coin) to be gold was asked, but this is trivially the same as the probability for the ball not to be silver (i.e. $1 - \frac{1}{3}$).

While the theory in this case is elementary (to quote Wikipedia, "This simple but counterintuitive puzzle is used as a standard example in teaching probability theory"), a computer simulation can show the same numerically for much more complicated scenarios. Here's your setup in R:

## Make three boxes
boxes <- list(box1=c("gold", "gold"),
              box2=c("silver", "silver"),
              box3=c("gold", "silver")) |> do.call(cbind, args=_)
#>      box1   box2     box3    
#> [1,] "gold" "silver" "gold"  
#> [2,] "gold" "silver" "silver"

set.seed(1)  ## For reproducibility

## Randomly pick one of the three boxes
box_picked <- sample(1:3, size=1E6, replace=TRUE)
#> [1] 1 3 1 2 1 3 3 2 2 3 ...

## From these boxes, take the balls in random order
balls <- lapply(box_picked, \(i) sample(boxes[,i])) |>
   do.call(rbind, args=_)
#>      draw1    draw2    
#> [1,] "gold"   "gold"  
#> [2,] "gold"   "silver"
#> [3,] "gold"   "gold"  
#> [4,] "silver" "silver"
#> ...   ...      ...

## Condition on a gold ball being picked first
gold_first <- which(balls[, 1] == "gold")
## Note that this is no longer the full sample space!
length(gold_first)
#> 500771   ## Basically N/2

## Probability that next ball is silver
mean(balls[gold_first, 2] == "silver")
#> [1] 0.333971   ## Very close to 1/3

To quickly address your final point: this is only a "paradox" in so far that the intuition of most people -- including your friends apparently! -- will not be correct. In that sense it isn't a true paradox, but more accurately a probability puzzle as described above. Wikipedia has a list of very similar problems, including Monty Hall's three doors which is identical.

Here's an efficient way to do some of the arithmetic involved: \begin{align} & \overbrace{ \left( \frac13, \frac13, \frac13 \right)}^{\begin{smallmatrix} \text{prior probabilities} \\ \text{of the three boxes} \end{smallmatrix}} \times \overbrace{\left( 1, \frac12, 0 \right)}^{\begin{smallmatrix} \text{probabilities of} \\ \text{a gold ball from} \\ \text{the three boxes} \end{smallmatrix}} \\[12pt] = {} & \underbrace{ \left( \frac13, \frac16, 0 \right) }_{\begin{smallmatrix} \text{term-by-term} \\ \text{product} \end{smallmatrix}} \propto \underbrace{\left( \frac23, \frac13, 0 \right) }_{\begin{smallmatrix} \text{term-by-term} \\ \text{product} \\ \text{“normalized,”} \\ \text{giving the} \\ \text{posterior} \\ \text{probabilities of} \\ \text{the three boxes} \end{smallmatrix}} \end{align} The “normalization” consists of multiplying all three components of this triple by the same number in order to make their sum equal to $1.$ In the term-by-term product their sum is $\frac13+\frac16+0=\frac12,$ so multiplying them all by $2$ makes their sum equal to $1.$

So the conditional probabilities of the three boxes, given that the one ball drawn so far was gold, are $2/3$ for the box with two gold bars, $1/3$ for the box with one gold and one silver, and $0$ for the box with two silver balls.

On the other hand, if you have put the ball back into the box, you get a different answer, a higher probability of getting a gold ball next time, since you've added a gold ball to the box by putting it back. It comes to $5/6.$

Probability is first and foremost mathematics, and then, hopefully, intuition.

MATHEMATICS

We want the probability of the event $\{G_1, S_2\}$ given $G_1$. By the fundamental probability theorem that links the three kinds of probabilities (Bayes's Law), $$\Pr \left(\left\{G_1, S_2\right\} \mid G_1\right) = \frac{\Pr \left(\{G_1, S_2\right\}, G_1)}{\Pr(G_1)}$$

Based on the (absolutely accurate) graph in the answer of @PBulls, $$\Pr(G_1) = \frac 1 3 + \frac 12 \cdot \frac 1 3 = \frac 12.$$

More over $$ \Pr \left(\{G_1, S_2\right\}, G_1) = \frac 1 6.$$

So $$\Pr \left(\left\{G_1, S_2\right\} \mid G_1\right) = \frac{\Pr \left(\{G_1, S_2\right\}, G_1)}{\Pr(G_1)} = \frac {1/6}{1/2} = \frac 1 3.$$

INTUITION ?

Intuition often misleads us in probability matters, and sometimes, it is like an optical illusion: even if we get to know what the real picture is the optical illusion does not necessarily disappear ---the neurological mechanisms of the eye do not totally yield to intellectual realizations.

In the current setting, we may be able to pinpoint what is the "optical illusion" that leads people to answer, in the specific situation, "the probability that the next ball is silver given that the first was gold is $1/2$" ---and not the correct $1/3$.

The thinking may go like this:

"We drew a golden ball from a box, and now we face the same box, that contains just one ball, either a golden or a silver. Therefore, the probability of drawing a silver is $1/2$."

The "either/or" set the stage for the illusion, because they verbally point towards "two equally likely outcomes", and this is reinforced by the fact that the description also goes "the next ball that we will take..." Together these verbal descriptions create the impression that we face a situation equivalent to yet another "random draw".

But there is no "random draw/choice" anymore. The box contains just one ball. Moreover, the silver/gold probabilities for this remaining ball have been affected by our previous choice, on which we now "condition" the situation. The fact that the remaining ball can be either gold or silver does not automatically mean that the probability of being either will be equal (and so 1/2). The fact that we do not straightaway "know" what this ball is, does not make these probabilities equal.

Yet another way that we can engage in misleading thinking is the following:

"Given that we drew a golden ball, we either face the purely golden box, or the mixed silver/golden box. We don't know ---hence, the probabilities are $50-50$ to be in either situation."

One could view both approaches as an example of a misguided application of the ("principle of indifference": if we don't know, we assign equal probabilities (the existing deeper criticism of the principle itself is not pertinent here). But in order to apply the principle of indifference validly (again, beyond the wider issues with it), requires the absence of any relevant information...

Why we may think that we have no "relevant information"? Because, by stating "we drew a golden ball (in the past) and given this, now we face...". we possibly create the (wrong) impression that "what is done is done, it affects the current situation only by making us face an "either/or" situation for which we know nothing about".

In other words, the very fact that affects the probabilities of the remaining ball being silver (the draw of the first golden ball) and makes them not equal, is also the fact that, when stated verbally, may reinforce the misguided intuition on the matter.

This is why putting verbal descriptions of probabilistic situations into mathematical form and then applying the rules of probability theory to obtain the answer, and then attempting to understand why the answer is what it is, is the wise way to go... I didn't say that the optical illusion disappeared, did I?

First, I would take the guidelines and Dr. Altman at their word: It does allow other researchers to understand the data better. And it does so easily: Just a few extra columns in a table.

Second, I very much agree with mdewey. It makes meta-analysis easier. How many studies use exactly the same covariates? Not many.

Third, it allows future researchers to compare their models to yours even if they used somewhat different covariates. Replication is good. Also, if they find unadjusted main effects that are quite different from yours then that may point to differences in the samples (or the populations from which they were drawn) that could be interesting. Even if your study manages to have a truly random selection from some well-defined and enumerated population (and that's not that common) it could be that your population (say, people living in the United States) is different from their population (say, people living in Bangladesh) in key ways that may be clearer in the main effects.

Fourth, covariates that are important in one population may be unimportant (or even kind of silly) in another. I recall one study, done in a very poor country, in which one key covariate was whether they had adequate supplies of soap. Asking about supplies of soap in (say) Denmark would not only be pointless, it would be kind of insulting.

Finally, and most generally, it is better to have more information.

Doug Altman was a medical statistician supreme. But in this particular case I think inclusion of unadjusted estimates is a bad idea because at their heart they assume homogeneous distributions (zero-width study inclusion criteria or non-existence of risk factors). Far from giving comfort to readers, unadjusted estimates do little but give them worry when adjusted estimates are not very close to adjusted ones. They start to cast doubt on the adjusted estimates, not on the faulty unadjusted ones. Only adjusted estimates account for outcome heterogeneity (whether or not confounding is present).

I would much rather see imperfect adjustment (e.g., acting as if there are only 3 prognostic factors) than unadjusted estimates (acting as if there zero prognostic factors).

The fact that meta-analysis is easier when not adjusting is true. It is simpler to do erroneous things.

What are the basic assumptions of simple proportions, empirical distribution functions, and Kaplan-Meier estimates? That the observations come from a single distribution (homogeneity).

To make a different argument: I think this discussion arises, fundamentally, not because there is a debate to be had about the merits of "unadjusted" estimates. I think talking about unadjusted as opposed to adjusted estimates is just not very compatible with what causal inference researchers want to do nowadays.

Most applied studies in quantitative causal inference try to estimate some type of contrast between treatment-specific means of the form $E[Y(a)]$. For a binary treatment, we could, for example, want to estimate an average treatment effect written as $E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]$, or a relative version $\frac{E[Y(1)]}{E[Y(0)]}$. It just so happens that, under a few assumptions, this quantity is identical to $E[Y | W, A = a]$, where $W$ is a sufficient adjustment set of confounders. The most intuitive way to estimate this is via regression, where we can estimate a regression model for the outcome and average over $E[Y | W = w, A = a]$ to estimate $E[Y(a)]$. This is what we refer to as the adjusted estimate. The same procedure, but omitting covariates $W$ from the regression model is often referred to as the unadjusted estimate.

But I would argue: if we use regression adjustment to estimate counterfactual quantities, this is only to estimate a causal target parameter. Contrasting adjusted and unadjusted estimates is arguing the wrong way around. It starts by positing an estimation procedure (regression adjustment), and maps it to a causal target parameter by coincidence (because, conveniently, regression adjustment is a method that works for this purpose). If one instead starts with the target parameter and asks themselves how to estimate it, it is more obvious that we seek an estimator of $E[Y | W, A = a]$, and that $E[Y | A]$ is unsuited for this purpose. This becomes especially clear in cases where one uses machine learning or stratifies estimates by treatment, in which cases there is no "unadjusted estimate". Clearly, the fact that no unadjusted estimate exists in such cases is not because the methods aren't appropriate, it is instead because the distinction between adjusted and unadjusted estimates is the wrong one to make.

I would argue the better way forward is by using other language. The adjusted estimate is instead an estimate of a causal target parameter. The unadjusted estimate is sample description (though, if the sample was representative, it could also be an estimate of the population risk of the outcome). This way, we put the research question first and allow ourselves to think hard about how to answer it.

One interesting little disagreement in this thread was between Peter Flom, who suggested that unadjusted estimates are easier for meta-analyses, and Frank Harrell, who would consider such meta-analyses erroneous. Both are clearly true; a meta-analysis of unadjusted estimates is completely inappropriate to estimate a causal target parameter, but it could (in an appropriately-designed study) instead be an estimator for a descriptive quantity we want to perform a meta-analysis for. So IMO we can resolve this disagreement by thinking about target parameters first.

Yes, $n$ is a statistic. We routinely use $n$ in calculations, such as $\bar X = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, so it is legitimate to just take the $n$ on its own.

(Truly weird is that a constant is a legitimate function of the data, so $4$ is a statistic, too, and often one that has a property called admissibility.)

In most cases, the sample size $n$ is an ancillary statistic; that is, it does not by itself alone give information about the parameter. In such cases it is mostly treated as a constant. See

  • Define "ancillary information" without referencing ancillary statistics

  • Can someone explain the concept of ancillary statistics in layman's terms?

Even if in a case $n$ is random, say you sample until funds dry out ... but if its distribution does not depend on parameters of interest, it is safe to treat as constant.

So interesting cases are when $n$ is not ancillary. Some examples:

  1. Observing a Poisson process for a fixed time $T$. Then $n \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda T)$ so its distribution clearly depends on the parameter, and, since $T$ is fixed, $n$ is sufficient.

  2. Sequential sampling until first success, leading to a geometric distribution.

  3. Adaptive clinical trials, with early stopping criteria. The sample size will be informative about the treatment effect

So, excluding sample size as a statistic will at least not be helpful! The answer by @Dave gives the formal reasons that sample size is a statistic, I have tried to show why that definition is necessary.

Yes, but also beware a complication

The answer is yes: the sample size is a statistic - it can be obtained from the data vector. Now, having said this, you should also beware of a slight complication to this, which is that some statistical discussions use the term "statistic" informally to refer to a sequence of statistics indexed by $n$. This is reasonably common in discussions of estimators and their properties, and especially common when discussing their asymptotic properties. In this case, the sample size is used as an index for a sequence of statistics.

For example, you will find some discussions of using the sample mean as an estimator for the true mean of a distribution. In this context, we might refer to the "statistic" for the sample mean $\bar{X}_n$, when we are formally referring to the full sequence $\{ \bar{X}_n | n \in \mathbb{N} \}$. By referring to the latter we can make generalised statements about its properties for all $n$ and we can make statements about its asymptotic properties when $n \rightarrow \infty$ (which is very common in discussions of estimators).

A. Under Bluman's definition: No

He defined statistic is obtained by using the data values from a sample. This implies two things:

  1. The data values from the sample should exist or be known first before the statistic. But for sample size, even when we don't know the numerical values of each observation yet, we always know how many data values we intend to collect or have collected.
  2. From a practical standpoint, if one or more data values from a sample is missing (unobserved, not just zero), standard statistics (like sample mean or variance cannot be computed directly without performing mathematical techniques such as data imputation. But again for sample size, let's say you have 20 observations (sample size) and 5 of those observations have missing data. Those missing values prevent you from numerically calculating sample statistics. But your sample size remains known as 20 regardless of whether you successfully recorded those data values or not.

B. Under Hogg's definition: Mathematically yes, but informationally a trivial statistic. (Applicable only on sampling methods where $n$ is fixed and pre-determined before the sampling process)

Definitions we need from Hogg's (p. 226):

  1. Sample size and data values

The sample observations have the same distribution as X [random variable], and we denote them as the random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, where $n$ denotes the sample size. When the sample is actually drawn, we use lower case letters $x_1,x_2,...,x_n$ as the values or realizations of the sample.

  1. Statistic (For convenience, recall the def from the question)

Let $X_1,X_2,...,X_n$ denote a sample on a random variable $X$. Let $T = T(X_1,X_2,...,X_n)$ be a function of the sample. Then $T$ is called a statistic.

Now, the question is can we mathematically represent $n = T(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n) $?

Technically, yes. From Hogg's definition of statistic, a statistic is defined as any valid function $T: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined on a sample space. Therefore, we can express $T(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$ as a constant function $T(X) = c$. (In other words, we can simply define a rule (a function) that maps the entire set of random variables (sample observations) as a tuple to $n$.)

Here's a concrete example: Let's say you have $10$ observations and the data values (realizations) are $\{3,4,6,9,1,5,8,7,15,12\}$.

According to Hogg, you can simply define a function mapping $T$ of every value as an entire tuple to the constant value of the sample size. And what makes it trivial is that mathematically, the example satisfies the formal def of the statistic, but practically, $T$ provides no useful information about the observed sample values ($X_i$) because $T$ simply outputs a fixed constant $n$ regardless of what the data values are.

C. Additional note on nuances (h/t @whuber)

While arguments on this answer strictly revolve around Bluman's and Hogg's definition as elementary statistics resources, they are insufficient in explaining the nuances from the standard mathematical definition. And so a measure-theoretic definition (Shao, 2003, pp. 100, 101) is as follows:

A measurable function of $X$, $T(X)$, is called a statistic if $T(X)$ is a known value whenever $X$ is known. In other words, the function $T$ is a known function.

In layman terms, let's say you have a known set of data values ($X$ is known). Again, using our concrete example, $\{3,4,6,9,1,5,8,7,15,12\}$. If you can create a function mapping to a certain property or value that depends only the observed data values themselves, then the function is a statistic.

"Observed" in the sense that we have the data as it is, and not something that we don't know the value or characteristic (unknown).

Any $T(X)$ is a random element. If the distribution of $X$ is unknown, then the distribution of $T$ may also be unknown, although $T$ is a known function.

And you don't need the (unknown) population distribution or parameters to obtain $T(X)$. You can construct $T$ that maps your sample data values to the sample size without knowing (or needing to know) the population mean, variance, standard variable or any other unknown properties of the population.

To better understand the distinction of a known function:

  • In probability/measure theory: A function is known if it is only dependent on "observed" inputs (no unknown parameters).
  • In other math fields: A function is known if it can be constructed/created.

Let's look at these two examples.

  • $f(X) = \bar{X}$ ($\bar{X}$ is a sample mean)
  • $g(X) = X - \mu$ ($\mu$ is a population mean)

Under probability/measure theory, $f$ is a known function but $g$ is not because you need an unknown parameter $\mu$ to find $g$. Yet on other math fields, both $f$ and $g$ are known because we have just constructed it.

So, looking back at our initial points from Bluman's definition:

Point 1: On point of data values from the sample existing or known before the statistic.

There are sampling approaches in which the sample size is not known beforehand and/or is not a fixed value and can vary throughout the selection process.

Scenario A: Sample size is not known. We can define a function that maps our data to our unknown sample size. In fact, this makes it not trivial because it provides information about the sample's properties.

Scenario B: Sample size is not fixed (variable). Same as scenario A, we can still define $T$ but now $T(X)$ becomes a random variable instead of just a fixed constant.

Point 2. On point of missing data.

While the initial point is taken from a practical standpoint, Shao's definition guarantees that you can still define a statistic even when missing data exists.

Conceptually: Missing data is a separate concern and is part of the data collection process, rather than the sample itself. Every observation on our sample inherently possess a true value $Y_i$ at the first place regardless of whether it is successfully recorded or not.

Mathematically: Missingness on data values can be defined as $X_i = (Y_i, R_i)$, where $R_i \in \{0,1\}$, where $0$ is unobserved and $1$ is observed) indicates whether $Y_i$ is successfully recorded. This implies that missing data doesn't "break" our ability to define a statistic because it only redefines the nature of our random variable $X$, but leaves $T(X)$ unaffected.

Hence,

  • Sampling methods with known and fixed a priori sample size $n$: Trivial statistic where n is a fixed constant.
  • Sampling methods with unknown/ variable sample size during the selection process: A non-trivial statistic, where $n$ is a random variable.

A test statistic is any measurable function $T \colon \Omega \to \mathbb R$ of a random sample:

$$T \colon \omega \mapsto T\left(X_1(\omega),\, X_2(\omega), \ldots X_n (\omega)\right).$$

The significance level $\alpha$ and the critical region $I_\alpha$ are defined such that

$$\mathbb P\left[T(\omega) \in I_\alpha \right] = \alpha.$$

If $T(\omega) = n$, for all $\omega \in \Omega$, then

$$T^{-1}\left(\{x_0 \}\right) = \begin{cases}\Omega, \quad \text{ if } x_0 = n, \\ \varnothing, \quad \text{ if } x_0 \neq n.\end{cases}$$

Both of these pre-images are of course measurable. In fact, the pre-image of any set is either $\Omega$ or $\varnothing$. This makes $T$ measurable, so it is a test statistic.

In all honesty, a better definition would be to refer to the collection of measurables $\{T_n\}_{n}$ a test statistic, because we usually deal with a family of $T$'s and worry about the behavior as $n \to \infty$.

A way to make a statistic "independent" of the sample size $n$ is to require that $T$ can only be an assignment

$$T \colon \operatorname{Meas}(\Omega, \mathbb R) \to \mathbb R$$

taking a measurable function $X \colon \Omega \to \mathbb R$ to some real number.

For example, the expected value is such a morphism

$$\mathbb E \in \operatorname{Hom}\left( \operatorname{Meas}(\Omega, \mathbb R), \mathbb R \right)$$

being defined by

$$\mathbb E \colon X \mapsto \mathbb E[X].$$

But such assignments $T(X)$ are usually rather called parameters of $X$, or parameters of the distribution of $X$, than being referred to as "statistics" themselves.

If there are repeated observations, as may be the case with designed experiments with replicates, the residuals can be decomposed into estimates of pure error and lack of fit.

If you assume that any nonlinearity in the 'true' relationship is smooth, you can use smoothing of the residuals to try to approximate any remaining structure in the data. This is often used as a diagnostic tool (on residual plots for example), but it can be used to try to produce an approximate lack of fit measure.

This is straightforward with one predictor. With multiple predictors the curse of dimensionality will soon tend to come up. However, you might simplify, for example by assuming that the model is additive, say, and look at whether smooths in each variable improve the fit, though there are other possibilities.

Many approaches to comparing a simple, typically finite-parametric model to a more general one are possible in different circumstances.

A related approach to those mentioned by Glen_b and cdalitz is to employ a generalized additive model (GAM) to identify and quantify systematic deviations from the linearity assumption. GAMs extend linear models by including flexible, data-driven smooth terms, allowing non-linear relationships between predictors and the response variable to be captured effectively.

The GAM can be fitted using the same predictors as the linear model. Each predictor can include a smooth term, such as $s(x_i)$, to represent possible non-linearities. This flexibility allows the model to capture systematic deviations that a purely linear model cannot. If a smooth term is statistically significant, it suggests that the linearity assumption may not hold for that predictor. Comparing metrics such as the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) or adjusted $R^2$ between the GAM and the linear model can also provide evidence of whether the GAM offers a substantially better fit.

The systematic error, $\epsilon_s$, introduced by the linearity assumption can be quantified using the smooth terms from the GAM. Specifically, the deviation between the observed data and the linear model can be expressed like:

$$ \epsilon_s = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ y_i - \hat{y}_{m}(x_i) - \hat{s}(x_i) \right]^2 $$

where $\hat{y}_{m}(x_i)$ is the model predictions and $\hat{s}(x_i)$ is the smooth term from the GAM.

Cosma Shalizi calls this "model specification testing" in his book Advanced Data Analysis from an Elementary Point of View. He advocates for testing along the following lines:

  1. Fit the parametric model (such as linear regression) to your data getting estimate $\hat{\theta}$ and in-sample mean squared error $\operatorname{MSE}(\hat{\theta})$.
  2. Fit a non-parametric model (such as kernel regression) to your data getting a regression function $\hat{f}$ and in-sample mean squared error $\operatorname{MSE}(\hat{f})$.
  3. Set $\hat{d} = \operatorname{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) - \operatorname{MSE}(\hat{f})$.
    • This measures how much better the non-parametric model fits than the parametric one.
  4. Simulate from the parametric model $b$ times to get fake data $(x_{ik}, y_{ik})$ where $i = 1, 2, 3, ..., n$ and $k = 1, 2, 3, ..., b$.
    • In the case of linear regression, where we do not model the distribution of the inputs, we will use $(x_{i}, y_{ik})$.
  5. Fit both the parametric and non-parametric model to the fake data obtaining estimates $\hat{\theta}_k$ and $\hat{f}_k$.
  6. Set $\hat{d}_k = \operatorname{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_k) - \operatorname{MSE}(\hat{f}_k)$.
    • These $\hat{d}_k$ values were simulated under the null hypothesis that the data generating process is given by the parametric model.
  7. The $p$-value of our observed value of $\hat{d}$ is approximately

$$ \frac{1 + |\{k: \hat{d}_k > \hat{d}\}|}{1 + b} $$

Note: we are adding $1$ to avoid reporting a $p$-value of $0$ in the event that there are no examples of $\hat{d}_k > \hat{d}$. Effectively we are inventing one fake such case and adding it in to both the numerator and denominator. This shouldn't matter much if $b$ is large.

We are asking "from the data simulated under the null hypothesis, in what fraction does the non-parametric model fit as much better than the parametric one, compared to our observed data?"

Classical hypothesis testing is an inductive version of the "proof by contradiction" - the asymmetry arises from the non-specific nature of the alternative hypothesis

In order to understand the asymmetry of a classical hypothesis test, it is useful to understand the broad logic of the test, which is essentially an inductive analogue of a proof by contradiction. In a proof by contradiction we begin with a null hypothesis, show that this leads logically to a contradiction, and therefore reject the initial premise that the null is true. In a classical hypothesis test, we begin with a null hypothesis, show that this leads to a highly implausible result in favour of the alternative (so not quite a deductive contradiction, but close), and therefore reject the initial premise that the null is true. If the null hypothesis is not found to be highly implausible, we do not reject it and it remains a plausible hypothesis.

Now, in principle, we could do the test either way around, taking one hypothesis as our assumed base and looking at the conditional probability of a result more in favour to the other hypothesis. However, it is typically the case that one hypothesis is highly specific and the other hypothesis is highly unspecific, such that it is easy to reliably specify conditional probabilities under the former, but difficult to do so under the latter. For example, we might have a null hypothesis that two variables are statistically independent and an alternative hypothesis that they are statistically dependent. The former hypothesis is very specific and has clear implications for conditional probabilities of particular results (e.g., pertaining to relevant test statistics). The latter is non-specific and does not have any clear implications for conditional probabilities of relevant test statistics - to obtain conditional probabilities we would have to specify how the variables are dependent in a very specific way. When we encounter a situation like this, the logic of the hypothesis test is simple and reliable to implement one way around, but it is highly tenuous to implement the other way around (because it requires specification of detailed assumptions that might be unreasonable).

The reason you find the Neyman-Pearson framework asymmetric, is because the Null Hypothesis test (NHT) is fundamentally asymmetric. And Type I and Type II errors are not symetrical.

When you make a Type I error, you are making an affirmative statement, which is in error. You are saying that the null can be rejected (and the alternative accepted), when in fact the null is true. To use Colquhoun’s language (here, or here), you “made a fool of yourself” and made an “unpublishable result publishable”, but you also fooled your audience. People who used your results to make decisions made the wrong decisions.

When you make a Type II error, by contrast, you just failed to make such an affirmative statement. You are simply saying that there is not enough evidence against the null to “safely” reject it (or said differently it would be foolish to reject the null based on the evidence). Now, it would be utter foolishness to interpret a non-significant test as grounds to “accept the null”, or even worse, as grounds to state that “the null is true”. But the fool here would not be the statistician, but the person making such unwarranted interpretations. So, at worst, you are unhelpful.

In the first case, you are leading your audience astray, and into an incorrect decision; in the other, you simply leave them with an indeterminate (but not false) answer. Not symmetric...

Note that if one is worried about Type II errors, a simple remedy is to use a larger sample size (yes, at the cost of more time and money spent). Interestingly, with this larger sample size, while your type II error rate decreases, your Type I error rate will stay exactly the same... Not symmetric...

I think of it as a “first do no harm” rule, but for statisticians; do not fool yourself, and your audience, even at the cost of missing a possibly significant result (just increase the sample size if it is that important).

Now, is the 0.05 significance arbitrary? Perhaps. Could one use .04, or .06, or even .01 or .1? Absolutely, even though they would be just as arbitrary (I have used .2 significance in submissions to FDA, without any pushback, for tests where Type I errors had minimal risks). And obviously .01 will cost you some power, and .1 will allow for more foolishness. If interested, you may want to read this paper, which shows that .05 is not so arbitrary after all, and that very similar values, and concepts, predate Fisher.

In principle, nothing in frequentism (i.e., frequentist understanding of probabilities) requires the asymmetry. My general interpretation of the Neyman-Pearson framework is not that "we should treat hypotheses asymmetrically", but rather "if we want to treat hypotheses asymmetrically for whatever reason, then we can use the N-P framework". You don't need to use N-P or general asymmetric hypothesis tests just because you work with a frequentist concept of probabitities. In fact, you can well use Bayesian methodology in that framework, or compute confidence intervals without running a test.

Asymmetric hypothesis tests have become very popular though (some think much too popular). I can see two somewhat opposite reasons for this.

  1. The first one is Popper's idea that in science we can only try to falsify hypotheses, not to verify them. Hypothesis testing can be seen as a probabilistic version of Popper's falsification logic. Assume that in the situation in question there is really only one research hypothesis of interest, and an all too unlikely result would "statistically falsify" it. The alternative hypothesis here would not be of primary interest, however according to the N-P approach, one could use the idea of an alternative to find an "optimal" test, i.e., a test that gives the best chance to actually reject the $H_0$ in case it is wrong. This theoretical setup requires that you specify the alternative, but it is not of primary interest, therefore not treated symmetrically. Important about this is that not rejecting the $H_0$ doesn't mean the $H_0$ is true, and if we want to adopt it as scientific "result"/current best explanation, we should try hard (more than once, in different ways) to reject it, so that we can say, at the end, that if the $H_0$ were wrong in critical ways, chances are we would have found that.

  2. In the literature we often find a very different use of hypothesis tests, namely where the null hypothesis is not the research hypothesis of interest, but rather a model for "randomness/nothing interesting going on/no influence of a factor" etc. The researcher is then often interested in showing the opposite, namely that something meaningful is going on. In this situation, rejection of the $H_0$ is often interpreted as "statistical proof" of the alternative, i.e., the research hypothesis that the researcher wants to show. But it certainly doesn't work as such a "proof", because rejection of the $H_0$ still allows for many distributions/models and can often be explained by issues such as biased sampling, data dependent decision making or (potentially hidden) multiple testing. The use that these tests have is to rule out (with some error probability) that the data are meaningless random noise, or the opposite, i.e., to inform the researcher that the data are in fact compatible with meaningless noise, and therefore do not license any interpretation that they are not. This is to some extent informative because human beings have a tendency to interpret meaning into meaningless noise, and tests of a "nothing is going on" $H_0$ give us a chance to distinguish what happens from random noise. Interpreted like this, again, we basically make an interpretation regarding the $H_0$ only, therefore asymmetry. The role of the alternative here is to specify in which way something meaningful may happen (i.e., our research hypothesis), once more choosing the test so that we have optimal power to reject in case the alternative obtains. Testing in this second way is particularly popular where we can't precisely specify the alternative because we have too imprecise knowledge. Testing a new medicine, we may be happy if we can show it does likely something good, but we couldn't specify in advance exactly how good it will be. Typically in such situations it is much easier to reject the null hypothesis rather than nailing down the precise effect (in many cases one can argue that it is too easy to reject the null, and the researcher should specify more precisely what they want to show rather than just rejecting a null hypothesis that in reality is pretty clear a priori not to hold). In any case, the null hypothesis is precise, therefore the situation is asymmetric.

One of the most direct ways to understand the harm of the asymmetry in frequentist inference is to consider the expected sample size needed to make a decision (e.g., consider 3 possible decisions: positive effect, negative effect, similarity) in the Bayesian vs. the frequentist paradigms when assessing evidence sequentially, i.e., admitting that sample size estimation is just a game. The Bayesian paradigm results in far less average sample sizes even without the use of external information, due to conservatism in frequentist sequential testing anchored on $\alpha$. This is exemplified with a simulation here where I’ll be soon adding the corresponding frequentist group sequential testing results.

The asymmetry in the frequentist approach exists because of

  • initial emphasis on 𝛼 in the false belief that it is an error probability, which makes some judges of the research put all their money on preserving $\alpha$, greatly down-weighting $\beta$ "error"
  • failure to respect decision theory, which shows us that consequences of decisions should be factored in
  • p-values as measures of data surprise under $H_0$ are not calibrated evidentiary measures
  • lack of a gray zone; unlike Bayesian posterior probabilities there is nothing in a p-value that informs the researcher there is insufficient information to make any type of decision (positive or negative). When a gray zone exists we see that a large number of analyses result in "no decision", which makes positive and negative decisions more meaningful when you can make them.

The reason is merely philosophical, and it relates to basically what science is. The null hypothesis is, in a sense, the absence of a pattern/constant that can be employed in a scientific theory, in fact the hypothesis "the treatment has no effect" is qualitatively different from the hypothesis "the treatment has a precise difference of 0.2 w.r.t the other treatment". In fact, if one wishes to test 2 different scientific theories, assuming that one of the 2 Is true, it would be quite weird to treat type 1 error and type 2 error asymmetrically.

There are also other indicators like the FDR which controls the expected number of false discoveries, but they are in fact not used as gold standard because they do not take actively into account the scenario where all null hypothesis are false.

By the way, as said, it is a philosophical reason which paradoxically hasn't, to my knowledge, discussed as one may wish for, and not every statistican in fact believes in this.

Before and After Scenario

I will first address the cases where the McNemar test is used on paired data (same subjects), and data is collected both Before, and After a Treatment (it is a very common way, but not the only way, the test is used: I will address the other ways further below).

  1. What does the McNemar test actually test?

Before the Treatment, the subjects fall into 1 of 2 possible, mutually exclusive, categories (Condition – $C$ -, or No Condition – $NC$ -). The proportion of subjects who have the Condition before is the Prevalence ($P_B$). The test asks whether the treatment effect is associated with the condition or not. The null is that the Treatment equally affects the $C$ or $NC$ subjects (and the alternative is that the Treatment has a different effect on the $C$ or $NC$ subjects).
The above null is equivalent to saying that there is “marginal homogeneity” (i.e. the sum of the first row of the 2x2 matrix is equal to the sum of the first column, and the sum of the 2nd row is equal to the sum of the 2nd column).
And the null is also equivalent to testing whether the 2x2 matrix is symmetric (i.e. the 2 non-diagonal counts are equal).
I will not attempt to try to explain why either of these 2 alternative presentations of the null would have an intuitive, practical application.

One can see the first issue right here; the McNemar does not test if a Treatment had an effect, it tests whether it had an effect which is associated with the Condition (i.e. it had an unequal effect on the $C$ or $NC$ subjects; said differently, it had a differential effect).
This is not so much a problem with the test, when properly understood, but a problem with how the test is presented in most sources, and how it is used.

For example, the first example of Wikipedia’s page on the McNemar test says

In this example, the null hypothesis of "marginal homogeneity" would mean there was no effect of the treatment.

This is incorrect; the null is that it has the same effect on $C$ and $NC$ subjects. The test then shows a very low p-value ($p<0.001). And Wikipedia concludes that;

Thus the test provides strong evidence to reject the null hypothesis of no treatment effect.

But in fact, in this example, the Treatment “cured” 54% of the initially affected subjects, but “infected” 64% of the unaffected subjects; so, proportionally, it did more harm to healthy subjects than it did good to sick subjects. And it is this difference between the 2 categories which triggered the significance of the test.
This explains the puzzlement of many (e.g. this question on CV), which see a significant McNemar, even though the “effect” affected only a very small proportion of subjects; This is because the test is not a test of effect, but a test of “differential effect” (different between the 2 categories). Which is to be expected, because it does not consider the concordant cells.

This example also gets us to the 2nd issue, the fact that the McNemar is not directional (because squaring the count difference gets rid of the sign). Basically, the McNemar is 2-sided, that is the null is simply that the effect is not equal for the 2 categories. But in a Before/After scenario, one has an a-priori direction, namely that the Treatment is beneficial (it would cure a disease, improve grades, etc.). By being 2-sided, it loses power over an alternative which could accommodate single-sided alternative hypotheses.

Let’s look at a simple example, where the Treatment affects $C$ and $NC$ subjects equally, namely “converting” the same (low) percentage (2%) of each group. The 2x2 matrix may look like:

The $\chi^2$ statistic is 0, the p-value is 1, as should be expected, since the effect is the same for both categories (2% change), the matrix is symmetric, the 2 non-diagonal counts are the same, etc. But say now that the condition was relatively rare, and so the initial prevalence (in the Before sample) is low. The matrix now may look like:

The McNemar test is now significant. But the effect is exactly the same as in the previous case (2% change regardless of the condition), only the prevalence changed?

This brings the 3rd issue, the fact that the McNemar test is affected by prevalence. Said differently, it is valid as a test of association (of the effect to the condition) if and only if the initial prevalence is .5 ($P_B = .5$). For any unbalanced prevalence, the McNemar test returns an incorrect answer. That, to me at least, starts to look like a fatal blow, because I have never seen a real world sample which was perfectly balanced between the 2 dichotomous categories. Hence, the McNemar is always biased somehow by the imbalance.

Let’s illustrate by a 3rd example: same scenario as before, but now the Treatment is associated with the condition (it “flips” 20% of the $C$ subjects, and still only 2% of the $NC$ subjects). The matrix may look like:

The test is not significant, which is absurd. And the reason is the 4th issue (with the 3rd issue being a consequence of this 4th issue), namely that the test is not a test of proportions (marginal or not), but a test of absolute counts. The test only looks at the difference between the 2 non diagonal cells. If we call these 2 cells $b$ and $c$ (see Wikipedia), the $\chi^2$ statistic is $\chi^2 = \frac {(b-c)^2} {(b+c)}$. This statistic only depends on the counts, and not the proportion of these counts relative to the initial prevalence, or any other such other count...

As a side note, in their original paper, Quinn and McNemar alluded to this assumption of equal prevalence.

If we wish a formula analogous to the preferred (2), that is, one involving an estimate based on the combined sets of responses or a p based on the total as a better estimate, we note that such a p would, as in the case of (2), imply that the population values for the two proportions are equal (emphasis mine). This would be consistent with the null hypothesis that p2 - p1=0, except for random sampling fluctuations.

The choice of words here is very interesting (and revealing). They chose to say that their test implies that the population proportions of the 2 categories are equal, rather than saying “assumes”? (as one can not change the 2 population proportions; they will be what they are). And so there indeed seems to be a critical assumption for the McNemar test to provide correct results, briefly (and not quite truthfully) mentioned in the original paper, and long since forgotten by all... (which I hope the above examples illustrate clearly).

  1. Can we “fix” the McNemar test?

At this stage I have become convinced (and I hope to have convinced a few others) that the McNemar test, comparing Before and After paired categorical data, should be obsoleted (to begin with it is not clear that a test of association of treatment to conditions is needed/interesting, but even if it is, the McNemar test, as is, is so fraught with issues -the prevalence one being the most critical-, that its results cannot be relied on).
So can it be fixed?

The answer is “Yes”. For that, we need to realize that the McNemar test can be replaced by a binomial Sign test, testing against the null hypothesis that the proportion $p=.5$. Several software in fact offer this “exact binomial test” as an alternative to the traditional $\chi^2$ test, and other continuity corrected versions of it. But if we used a Sign test as found on these software packages, it would suffer from the same issues (test of association of the effect to the condition instead of test of an effect, affected by prevalence, test of counts not proportions), except the 2nd (we can run single-sided binomial tests).
The idea is not to test against $p=.5$ but to test against $p=P_B$, i.e. against the Before (initial) prevalence.

It should be clear that if we have a lot more $C$ subjects to begin with (or $NC$ subjects), then our chances of the Treatment flipping them are much higher than for the other category. And thus that testing against $p=.5$ is not appropriate.

Let’s look at the 3rd matrix (where McNemar said “no association” even though the effect was much stronger on the -under-represented- $C$ subjects). I now added a single-sided binomial test, testing the observed discordant counts against the prevalence ($H0 \text {: effect on C} \le P_B= \frac {50} {550} = .9091$.

While McNemar says “absolutely no association”, the binomial says “strong association”. It is comparing 10 (C->NC) out of 20 (sum of all discordant counts) against the prevalence $P_B=50/550=0.9091$, and testing the null that $p \le P_B$ against the alternative $p > P_B$ (one sided test). The p-value for this is $p=0.000003$.\

This “modified” Sign test still does not look at the concordant counts (but it takes them into some account by using the prevalence), it is single sided (because we want to show that the treatment has an effect in the “right” direction), and it does not look at counts, but actual proportions.
Now, for those who do not like exact binomial tests, you can instead use a single-sided z-test of proportions, comparing the proportion of “good” discordant counts (the ones with the effect we want) over all discordant counts, to the prevalence in the before sample. It solves the same 4 issues of the McNemar test that the Sign test solves; whether it is a good approximation of binomial proportions is a topic left for another post.

The first point to address is what kind of 2x2 matrix is being used. I have seen at least 2 types being used in articles, textbooks, etc.

The first -association, not effect- is less clear in this context). The 5th issue is that this approach has no association to the ground truth. We compare what each test called positive or negative, w/o any care to whether this was a true positive, or a false negative, etc...Surely, nothing very good could come of this In this case.

So we need to conclude that using the McNemar test as a single 2x2 matrix, comparing positive and negative results of 2 diagnostic tests is simply very poor practice; such a test can not yield any reliable result.

  1. Comparing sensitivity and specificity

Another common way to use the McNemar test for dichotomous tests is to separately compare the sensitivities, and specificities of the 2 tests, using 2 2x2 matrices.
In the following discussion, I will only consider comparing sensitivity, but whatever applied to sensitivity will equally apply to sensitivity.
Note also that now, we have a link to the ground truth; we compare sensitivity only on subjects we know are actually positive.
Note further that we no longer have a prevalence issue (because the comparison between positive cases is not affected by the relative number of positive cases in the sample). This eliminates the most critical issue found in the Before/After discussion.
And because the prevalence issue is no longer present, an unmodified Sign test should be used (comparing against $p=.5$). In the test results below, I still use a single-sided Sign test, because the expectation is that Test2 is “better”.

The McNemar still is double-sided, but one could always use a z-test (on the discordant counts) to obtain an equivalent single sided test.

Conclusion

  1. When used for a Before/After scenario, the McNemar test is not a test of “effect”, but a test of “differential effect” (the effect of the test is different for the 2 categories).
    However, even if properly understood as a test of differential effect, the standard McNemar test should not be used for Before/After scenarios, as it gives erroneous results as soon as the initial prevalence of conditions in the Before state is not .5.
    Instead, it should be replaced by a Sign test (possibly single sided), testing against the prevalence (and not .5, as the standard McNemar test does) (or an equivalent z-test).
  2. The standard McNemar test can be used to compare the sensitivities and/or specificities of 2 dichotomous diagnostic tests. In this scenario, it actually tests for equal sensitivities (or specificities) between the 2 diagnostic tests, and does not suffer from the prevalence issue.
  3. The McNemar test can not be used to compare test outcomes (positive and negative test results) between 2 dichotomous diagnostic tests. This yields absurd results.

Note 1: all the 2x2 matrices are “ideal” matrices under each of the scenarios. Of course, real world matrices would have some sampling noise added to them. But idealized matrices were used for the simplicity of the examples.

Note 2: some contributors may disagree with my characterization of the $\chi^2$ test as “double-sided”. I am fully aware that the $\chi^2$ test only considers a single tail of the statistic’s distribution (the right tail); so in that sense it is single-tailed. But it considers both sides, of the difference of counts; in that sense it is double-sided. That choice of words is not an error, or a confusion, but was cautiously chosen to in fact avoid confusion.
